activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
The kettle had been on for ten minutes before Emile noticed it, and by then the kitchen smelled of scorched metal and his grandfather's tea was ruined for the second time that afternoon. Emile sat at the table with his chemistry notebook open, the same page of wrong answers in front of him, the ones his teacher had marked in red pen with a single note: see me. He didn't want to see anyone. He wanted to sit in this kitchen, where the light came through the lace curtains and landed on the checked cloth in little diamonds, and figure out how he had gotten every single question wrong.

"You're boiling something," his grandfather said from the doorway, saturnine as always, his face giving away nothing but a certain dry amusement. "And it isn't just the kettle."

"Equilibrium," Emile said. "It's for the retake on Monday." He slid the notebook across the table. "These are the ones I missed."

His grandfather put on his glasses, which hung from a chain of fake gold, and bent over the page. He had been a machinist for forty years and could read a blueprint the way other men read newspapers, but chemistry was foreign territory. Still he looked, and turned the page, and looked again, while Emile rescued the kettle and refilled it and set it back on the burner with exaggerated care, as if the stove might notice him this time.

The problems were all the same kind. A reaction at equilibrium, a table of data, then a change: heat the flask, cool the flask, add more of one gas, take some away. Predict the shift. Emile had done what his notes told him to do. A system at equilibrium resists a change, shifts to counteract it, finds a new position. He had treated the heating and cooling exactly like the additions and removals, the same moves in a different direction. And all the temperature answers were wrong, only those, every one, while the others he had gotten right.

He remembered, then, a night in October, his mother driving him home from the tutoring center he had since stopped attending. The tutor had said something as they were packing up, some colloquialism about the system pushing back, and Emile had laughed and repeated it to his mother in the car, and she had laughed too, and neither of them had been thinking about what the words actually covered. He had liked the phrase. It had felt like understanding. He had carried it into the exam like a coin he assumed was currency everywhere, and it had turned out to be good in some shops and worthless in others.

The kettle began its low whine. Emile poured water over the tea bags and watched the color extrude itself from the leaves in slow ribbons, dark into pale, and it struck him with an almost physical certainty that he had been treating two different things as one. Adding or removing a substance, changing a pressure: these pushed the system to a new position, the same balance reestablished, the same numbers holding. But temperature was not a push from outside the balance. It reached into the balance itself and rewrote it. The ratio, the whole relationship between forward and reverse, took on a new value, one that his table of constants no longer described. When he had heated the reaction and then used the same K, he had been reading an old map in a country whose roads had moved.

He sat down and worked the temperature problems again from the beginning, saying it aloud under his breath: of the common disturbances, only a change in temperature changes the value of K. The additions, the removals, the pressure changes, all of those leave it alone. His pen moved fast, and when he finished, the answers that had been wrong were right, and the ones that had been right stayed right, and the page for the first time looked like something he had done rather than something done to him.

From the doorway, the old man watched him without speaking. He had raised a son who had raised this boy, and he had watched both of them make the same face over homework, the jaw set, the pen tapped twice against the table. He could not follow a line of it. But he knew the look of a person who had gone from lost to found in the space of a cup of tea, and he thought it was worth standing still for, worth the cold tea, worth pretending he had come in for something else. Whether the boy would keep this or lose it again by Monday, he could not say. Nothing ever stayed solved in this house for long.

"Do you want a second cup?" Emile asked, already reaching for the kettle. His grandfather sat down across from him and pushed the notebook back to his side of the table.

"Explain it to me," he said. "The whole thing. I've got until the water boils."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows, so 100 customers and 1,000 orders produce 100,000 rows.
story:
I have never been the kind of person who panics, which is why the library laptop freezing did not faze me at all. I pressed the power button and held it, the way my brother taught me, and while the screen went black I told myself the query had been correct. It was a LEFT JOIN, or something like it, between a customers table and an orders table, and all I wanted was the list of customers who had never ordered anything. Mr. Alvarez's practice database had a hundred customers in it and a thousand orders. I knew that because I had counted them the day before, sitting in the third-floor study room of the public library with my notebook open, feeling like someone with a lineage of programmers behind her, even though my mother cleaned offices and my father drove a van and neither of them had ever written a line of code.

I was not impecunious, exactly. I had thirty-four dollars in my account and a bus pass. But the coding boot camp in the spring catalog cost four hundred, and the library's free database class met on Thursdays at four, and so Thursdays at four was where I was. Mr. Alvarez, who taught it, had a way of proselytizing about SQL that I privately found exhausting, though I sat in the front row every week and took notes in blue pen.

That Thursday the laptop in front of me displayed my query. I had typed it fast because the room closed at five and I wanted to print my results. When I ran it, the little spinner appeared, and then the fan came on, loud in the quiet room, and then nothing moved at all. I waited. A boy two seats over, Desmond, leaned toward my screen.

"You didn't put an ON," he said.

"I did," I said, because I was sure I had. I am careful with syntax. I scrolled up in the editor, and there it was: JOIN orders, and then straight to SELECT. No ON clause at all. The join had nothing to match on, so it was matching everything to everything, which Desmond explained while I stared at the frozen spinner. "A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows," he said. "A hundred customers and a thousand orders, that's a hundred thousand rows." He said it flatly, not smugly, which somehow made it worse. The laptop was trying to build a hundred thousand rows for a girl who wanted seventeen names.

Here is what actually happened, though Sienna would tell it differently later, and did, to Mr. Alvarez, and to her brother on the phone. She forced the machine off, waited, turned it back on, and when the session restored she opened her query again and read it out loud, slowly, from the top. She found the missing line. She wrote ON customers.id equals orders.customer_id, and under it she typed her condition, and she ran it, and the results pane filled with seventeen customer names, each of them paired with a blank where an order should have been. She printed the list. Her hands were steady. If she tells you she was calm the whole time, that part is true; if she tells you she knew the ON clause was missing the moment the fan came on, that part is not.

I took my printed list to the front desk because the printer there is the only one that works, and while it ground out the page I read the names. M. Okafor. D. Reyes. Twice, the same name twice, which meant the database had two customers with the same name or a duplicate row, and I could not tell which from where I stood. The list was correct according to the query. The query was correct according to the syntax. And still I stood there unable to say whether M. Okafor had truly never ordered anything, or whether the orders table was missing a row somewhere, or whether there were two M. Okafor. Mr. Alvarez would say the answer was another query. I believed him, mostly.

Desmond came up behind me to collect his own printing. "You got the seventeen," he said.

"Some of them might be wrong," I said.

He looked at the page. "The query's right," he said. "The data might not be."

I folded the list and put it in my notebook, between the page where I'd counted the customers and the page where I'd counted the orders. Outside it was starting to get dark at four-thirty, the way it does in November, and the bus came every twenty minutes. On the ride home I opened my notebook on my knee and wrote at the bottom of the printout, in blue pen, "check duplicates." Then I wrote underneath it, smaller, "ask about NULL," though I did not yet know what that meant. The bus turned onto Halsted and I kept writing.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
Isabelle had claimed the third-floor bathroom at the community center for twenty minutes, which the schedule taped to the door said she was allowed to do, and which she needed, because in twenty minutes she would stand in front of eleven other peer health trainees and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections, none of which she had ever said out loud to anyone except her own reflection.

She spread her materials along the edge of the sink: the clinic's folder on contraceptive methods, the flowchart about affirmative consent, and the sheet about minors and testing that she had read four times on the bus and still half-believed. In the mirror her mouth moved through the opening she had rehearsed, something about how consent has to be freely given and can be withdrawn, and the fluorescent light buzzed so steadily that it felt like a second heartbeat in the room.

The door opened before she reached the contraception part. Dana came in with her jacket zipped to her chin even though it was June, and sat down on the radiator cover without asking why Isabelle was talking to the mirror.

"I have to tell you something and you can't look at me while I say it," Dana said, staring at the hand dryer instead. "Maybe you already know. From the way Marcus was at Kayla's party."

Isabelle turned around, and then, because Dana had asked, turned back toward the mirror, so that they were both facing the glass and could see each other without looking directly.

"Okay," Dana said. "We didn't, like, everything. But enough that I want to get checked, and I called the clinic, and they said come in, and then I panicked because my mom has to sign everything, for school, for the dentist, everything. She'd find the form. Or the insurance thing would come in the mail. So I was just going to not go."

"You were going to not go," Isabelle repeated, slowly, testing the weight of it. She picked up the sheet about minors and testing, the one the clinic nurse had handed out at the first training session, and read it again with the specific hunger of someone whose friend's face in the mirror had gone pale and still.

"Listen," she said. "All fifty states and Washington, DC, allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission. Some states set a minimum age, but that's the only catch. It's not a form thing. It's the law, it's written right here, this is from the clinic." Dana's shoulders came down maybe an inch. "I'm not saying it's nothing to think about, how you'd pay, what you'd do with the results. I'm saying the door is open, and nobody's mother is standing in front of it."

"You're sure," Dana said, though it wasn't really a question, and Isabelle understood that what she wanted was not more proof but permission to believe the proof she already had.

At that moment Mrs. Okafor, who ran the training, interposed herself through the half-open door with her clipboard and her effusive, carrying voice, announcing that they were starting in two minutes and that Isabelle, as the youngest trainee, would be warmly received, and was she planning to hide in the bathroom all afternoon like some kind of reluctant epicure of privacy? Dana laughed at that, a real laugh, wet at the edges, and Mrs. Okafor, catching sight of her face in the mirror, said nothing further and withdrew as gently as she had appeared.

"You can come with me," Isabelle said. "Saturday. We'll take the 12 bus, I know the building, and afterward there's the place with the mango smoothies, and you can tell me everything or nothing, whatever you want, that's actually the whole first thing I'm supposed to say in there." She gathered the papers, squared them against the counter, and watched Dana in the glass decide something.

"Okay," Dana said, and unzipped her jacket the rest of the way. "Okay. Say your consent speech to me one more time on the stairs, I'll be your practice audience." She held the door, and Isabelle walked through it still holding the sheet with the law on it, folded once, in her back pocket.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The gym smelled of varnish and the cold that came off the bleachers, and Ashton had until Friday to make the one-act watchable. Ms. Reyes had given him the script, three actors, and the gym stage after fourth period, then gone to her office to grade essays. Everything else was his. He stood at the edge of the stage with the script rolled in his fist and realized he had no idea how to tell people where to stand.

The trouble announced itself within ten minutes. Priya and Marcus played a couple arguing in a living room, and the script called for a sofa. There was no sofa, so they used a folded mat with a janitor's rag draped over it, and Priya sat on it while Marcus circled. Every time they ran the scene, the mat drifted. Marcus leaned on it, Priya dragged it when she rose, and by the third run the living room had migrated six feet toward the basketball key. "You're in the bleachers now," Devon said from the front row, where he sat with the light board he wasn't yet allowed to touch.

Ashton tried directing the way he had seen it done in films, which was to say louder and more general things. "Stay upstage," he called, and Priya asked which one was upstage. He said the back, and she said the back of what, the mat moves. He walked out, set the mat where he wanted it, ran back to his mark, watched it migrate again. Marcus offered to hold it still with his foot during his lines. That was the moment Ashton understood the problem was not the actors. It was that nothing on the floor told anyone where anything belonged.

He found the solution in the drama cabinet while looking for something else entirely, a roll of yellow tape, narrower than duct tape, beside a box of gaff. He brought it to Devon, who took it like a question. "That's spike tape," Devon said. "You mark the floor with it. Where furniture goes, where actors stop." Ashton tore a strip, knelt, and put a yellow T at each corner of the mat. He ran two more strips to the places Priya and Marcus kept ending up, small bright crosses on the gray boards, and stood back. The stage looked annotated, like a page someone had already studied.

The next run was different in a way he could see before he could name it. Priya hit her cross on the word "never," and Marcus, blocked into his own taped line, had to turn away from her at the moment the script said he lied, and the turn landed harder than any line reading Ashton had gotten out of him all week. Ashton had read, in the one directing book the library held, that blocking was supposed to historicize a scene, to place it, and he had thought the word meant something academic and distant. Watching Marcus's feet find the tape, he decided it meant something closer to the opposite. The marks were small and yellow and new, and they made the scene feel as if these movements had always existed, waiting to be found.

Priya had her own idea, and it did not match his. She thought the crosses made her mechanical, that she was performing geography instead of grief. "I can feel myself aiming for the tape," she said, sitting on the mat during the break, picking at one corner of it with her shoe. "It's like the scene has this vestigial skeleton now, and I'm walking on the outside of it." Devon said that was the point, that the skeleton held you up so the rest of you could fall apart. Priya said that was the dumbest thing he'd ever said, but she said it without heat, and Ashton let them argue while he looked at the crosses.

He had been reading phenomenology in his elective, a word his professor used for the study of how things show up to a person, and it had seemed, in the classroom, like a word that could never leave the classroom. But standing in the gym he could see the two positions plainly. From where Devon sat, the taped floor was a floor, and freedom lived inside it. From where Priya sat, the tape was a wall she kept brushing. Both of them were describing the same strips of yellow, and he could not prove either one wrong, and he suspected the truth was that the tape was doing both jobs at once, holding her and hemming her, and that no amount of directing would separate the two.

He tore up one cross, the one farthest from the mat, and pressed a new one a foot closer to Priya's side. "Compromise," he said. "You get the diagonal. If it still feels like aiming, we take them all up and start over." Priya looked at the new mark, then at him, and didn't agree or refuse. "Run it," she said, and stood, and Marcus unfolded himself from the bleachers, and Devon's hand went to the light board even though the lights weren't rigged yet, hovering there, ready. Ashton stepped back to his spot on the floor, found the scuffed place where his sneakers had worn their own small mark without anyone taping it, and called places.

"Places," Marcus echoed, and hit his yellow line.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
The rehearsal space was a converted church basement with taped lines on the floor where a riser used to be, and Victor had been given it every afternoon from two until four. His one-act, twenty-two pages about two brothers waiting out a storm, was his own script, and on Monday he had watched two actors walk into each other in scene two like men in a hallway mirror. Marcus went left when Dana went left, both corrected, and their shoulders met with a thud that stopped the scene dead.

"You planned this?" Dana asked, rubbing his arm.

Victor had not planned it. He had imagined the play mostly as voices, as pages, and the bodies had been an afterthought. That night in the dorm he wrote on the back of his script: figure out where people stand and when they move, before rehearsal, not during. On Tuesday he brought a scale drawing of the stage, marked the taped lines, and penciled small arrows for every entrance and cross. Marcus looked over his shoulder at the arrows and said, "What's that called, blocking?" and Victor said, "That's what it's called," though he had only learned the word from a library book the night before, a chapter about how the director sets where the actors stand and move during rehearsals.

It worked, mostly. Scene two no longer produced collisions. But a new problem arrived, quieter and harder to name. The actors stopped looking at each other. They hit their marks like students changing classes, and the storm scene, which had been raw when they stumbled through it on Monday, went smooth and empty. Dana delivered the line about their father with his eyes on the tape.

Victor sat in the third row after Tuesday's run and did not give notes. This was what he had wanted, in a way: control, the play obeying him. The other student directors at the camp were mostly effusive in rehearsal, praising everything, and Victor had privately thought their warmth was a kind of sophistry, flattery in place of decisions. He had decided he would be exact instead. Now exactness had given him a play that ran on rails and said nothing.

The subtext he could not ignore was Marcus. Marcus had applied to direct a one-act himself, and the camp had given the slot to Victor, and everyone in the basement knew it. Marcus had said congratulations the day the list went up, twice, which was once more than he needed to. When Victor asked him to try a cross downstage of the table, Marcus did it perfectly, without comment, and the perfection itself had a temperature.

On Wednesday Victor tried an experiment. He kept the blocking, every arrow, but told the actors to hold a beat before each move, to let the line land before they went. "Move when you have to, not when the paper says," he told them. It was a compromise he could not fully defend: the arrows delimited where they could go, and the holding opened a space inside those limits, and he did not know which was doing the work. Probably both. Probably neither alone.

Dana took the beat before the cross in scene four, and for the first time Marcus had to wait for him, had to stand in the silence with his hands open, and something passed between the brothers that was not in the script. Victor wrote nothing down. He watched it happen again, and it happened again, smaller the second time, which he suspected was how it worked, and he would have to learn to protect it without pinning it.

After the run, Marcus stayed behind to stack chairs. He stacked them evenly, not hurrying, and when he got to the last row he said, without turning around, "The waiting thing. That was good."

"You want to try it with the entrance in scene six?" Victor said.

Marcus turned around, holding one chair off the stack, like he hadn't decided yet where it went.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In the United States and many other countries, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered.
story:
Mason had written his ten-minute play on the backs of three cafeteria menus, and by Thursday afternoon he had reason to believe that Dana Okafor had photographed them while he was at the vending machine. Dana was directing her own piece in the showcase, a monologue about her grandmother's garden, and she was also the kind of person who read everyone's drafts over their shoulders and then prognosticated, cheerfully, which ones would get picked for the county festival. She had looked at his menus twice during lunch. Nobody looks at cafeteria menus.

The showcase was tomorrow night at seven. The auditorium was booked for rehearsal until six, which meant every one of the eleven campers needed a slot on the stage, and Ms. Ferreira had taped a sign-up sheet to the piano where the slots were disappearing faster than anyone could plan. Mason got the four o'clock slot, forty minutes, which sounded generous until he counted what had to happen in it: blocking, a lighting conversation with Pavel in the booth, and a run-through with two actors who had learned their lines off a photocopy he'd made that morning.

The play was about the night his father missed his seventeenth birthday dinner because of a flight delay in Denver, and about the taxi driver who ended up eating the extra plate of pasta. Mason had worried it was too small a subject. Dana had said, without looking up from her own script, that small subjects were all anyone in that room had, so he might as well be precise. He was trying to be precise. He had rewritten the taxi driver's monologue four times, and each version was on a different menu, which meant his play existed in pieces scattered across a table in the back row of the auditorium like some ridiculous genealogy of drafts, each one begetting the next.

At three thirty, he couldn't find the second menu. He searched his backpack, the table, the gap between seat cushions where the camp stored its ancient popcorn. Priya found him doing this and asked what he'd lost, and he told her, and then, because she was the only person he trusted in that building, he told her the rest: that he thought Dana had photographed the menus, and that if his play was good, she could type it up tonight and call it hers, and what could he even do about it, since his script was handwritten on trash and hers would look like a real script, and he didn't have money to register a copyright by tomorrow even if he knew how.

Priya frowned at him the way she frowned at wrong answers in math. "You don't register it," she said. "A play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it's written down. Here, and in a lot of other countries. That's the whole thing."

Mason said that couldn't be right, because then why did people put copyright symbols on things, and she said she didn't know, maybe because people liked symbols, but the protection didn't wait for them. She had looked it up in June after a boy at her old school took a song she'd written. Mason asked how that had gone. She said the boy had denied it and her mother had emailed his mother and it had been miserable, and the protection hadn't fixed any of that, it had just meant she could prove the song had been hers. He understood, then, that the fact was both a floor and not a ceiling: it existed whether or not he trusted it, and it would not walk across a stage and defend him.

He found the second menu at four ten, folded inside the photocopy Pavel had been using as a bookmark. It was his own handwriting, his own carelessness, and he stood in the aisle holding it while his actors waited on stage and Dana watched from the third row with what might have been guilt or might have been boredom. He walked down during the blocking and handed her the menu himself. "If you want to read it," he said, "read it while I can see you." She turned pink at the edges, said she'd only been looking at the dessert options, and he said he understood, the dessert options were the best part of the menu.

The run-through was rough. The actor playing the taxi driver kept swallowing his lines, and the lighting cue for the empty chair at the dinner table came late, so that for four full seconds Mason's whole play sat in bright, ordinary light, the chair looking less like an absence and more like furniture. He stood in the back row with his auxiliary script, the clean copy he'd typed at midnight, marking the cue in pencil, and he noticed Dana had left, and he noticed that he had stopped caring whether she'd photographed anything. The menus were his. The typed pages were his. What she did with either one was a problem with a shape now, not a shadow.

At five fifty, Ms. Ferreira called places for the last slot, and Mason sat in the front row with his pages in order, first draft to fourth, and drew a small copyright symbol on the top one, not because it needed it, but because he liked the way it looked, and he was eighteen and allowed to like things. Pavel's voice came down from the booth. "House to half, Mason." The lights on stage dimmed to a warm amber, and somewhere behind him the auditorium doors opened with their long hydraulic sigh.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
The blood pressure machine at Ridgeline Pharmacy had printed its receipt in thin gray type, and Kaylee's father had folded it twice and put it in his shirt pocket like a parking stub. She had seen the numbers before he folded it: 125 over 78. On the drive home he called it "fine, basically fine," in the voice he used when he wanted a subject closed, and Kaylee, who had a health project due Friday on interpreting vital signs, said nothing, which was its own kind of lie.

The project wanted her to explain a reading, name its category, and describe how diet and exercise could change it. She had the explanation half-organized in her notebook, but the category part had a hole in it. Her notes said something about a guideline from 2017, some American one, and a word she had written and underlined twice: elevated. She could not remember what it meant exactly, only that it sat somewhere below the word she did not want to say in the same sentence as her father.

At home she took the folded receipt from the laundry basket where his shirt had ended up, carried it upstairs, and locked herself in the bathroom because it was the only room with a door her brother respected. She sat on the edge of the tub with her phone, the receipt flattened on her knee, and looked it up. Under the 2017 American guideline, she read, elevated blood pressure meant a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80. She read it three times, mouthing the numbers.

So she did the arithmetic out loud, because saying things made them real for her in a way reading did not. "Systolic's the top one. 125. That's between 120 and 129." She checked the second condition against her fingers, like a bouncer at a door. "Diastolic's 78. That's below 80." She sat with that for a second. Her father's reading fit both parts, exactly, the way a key fits a lock you didn't want it to fit.

She stood and practiced at the mirror, because the project required her to explain it aloud, and because explaining it aloud was how she figured out whether she believed it. "If your systolic is 125 and your diastolic is under 80," she told her reflection, "then under the 2017 American guideline that's called elevated." The word sounded smaller in the bathroom than it had in her notebook. She said it again. "Elevated. Not the bad word. Just elevated." She was aware that she was negotiating with a category, as if the guideline were a person who might accept a bribe.

Her brother knocked. "Kaylee, I have to pee."

"Two minutes."

"You said two minutes yesterday and it was like ten."

"Mom made pasta," she called. "It counts."

Through the door he asked what she was doing, and she heard herself tell him, the whole thing, the pharmacy machine and the cuff squeezing his arm with what he'd called bellicose enthusiasm, and the numbers, and the category. Saying it to Owen was easier than saying it to the mirror. Owen was nine and repeated things with terrible accuracy, so she made him say it back. "The top number's between 120 and 129," he recited through the door, "and the bottom one's under 80, and the guideline's from 2017, and it's called elevated." She let him in.

The hard part had a shape now, and the shape was her father. He had folded the receipt because he did not want the numbers to become a family conversation, and she understood that; she also understood that walking his reading to him was going to feel, to him, like she'd been auditing his life. She thought of her English teacher describing the denouement of a novel, the part after the climax where consequences settle onto people, and she thought: this is that part, except in real life you sometimes have to walk into it on purpose, before it settles on its own.

She found him in the kitchen rinsing the pasta pot. She put the receipt on the counter between them, unfolded, and turned it so the numbers faced him, and said, "I looked it up for my project. It's called elevated. Not high. It means your top number is between 120 and 129, and the bottom is below 80, under the 2017 American guideline. Yours is 125 over 78." She kept her voice level, the way she'd practiced, though her hands were not level at all, so she put them in her pockets.

Her father looked at the receipt for a long moment, water dripping off his fingers onto the counter. "So not the bad word," he said.

"Not the bad word." She had the next part ready, the part about walks after dinner and what he put in the shopping cart, about how the project said these things could bring numbers down, though the project also said, and she was honest with herself about this, that she didn't fully understand the mechanisms yet, only the direction. She was still deciding how much of that uncertainty to say out loud.

"Sit down," her father said, and pulled out the chair beside him, and tapped the receipt with one wet finger. "Tell me the part about the walks again, slower."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Sarah's mother had signed the permission form without reading it, which was either trust or indifference, and Sarah had decided not to investigate which. The form said she could train as a peer health educator at the community clinic on Saturday mornings, and the clinic had sent home a manual the size of a phone book, which was why she was now at the kitchen table on a Tuesday night, highlighting the word "consent" for the fourth time.

"You're not actually going to teach people that," said her sister Natalie from the doorway. Natalie was thirteen and wanted, as far as Sarah could tell, to be wherever Sarah was, except when Sarah wanted her there. "Like, stand up in a room and say it out loud."

"Not stand up. It's a hotline. People call and I answer." Sarah turned the manual sideways, as though the chapter might make more sense rotated. "And I have to pass a practicum first. Saturday I explain contraception to a nurse and she decides if I sound like an idiot."

Natalie dragged a chair over and sat down anyway, which was its own kind of answer. She picked up the clinic pamphlet spread among the highlighters, the one with the cheerful cartoon clinic on the front, and read it with the slow suspicion she brought to anything Sarah cared about. "What's chlamydia?"

"An infection you can get." Sarah took the pamphlet back, then, feeling the smallness of that move, handed it back. "Here. You can read it. It's better you learn it from paper than from some idiot at school."

The idiot at school was, in fact, the reason Sarah had signed up at all, though she hadn't said this to anyone. In March her friend Dana had come over, sat on this same kitchen floor, and excoriated herself for an interminable hour over a boy who had said one thing in October and a different thing in February, and Sarah had discovered that she had nothing useful to say. She had held Dana's hand and offered tea and felt, for the first time in their friendship, completely useless. That was the gap the manual was supposed to fill. Saturday morning, on the practice line, she had explained consent to a bored staff volunteer, stumbled through the difference between the pill and condoms, and been told she was "adequate, which is what we look for." The testing chapter was the one she couldn't get right.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Dana.

"Question," Dana said, without hello. "That clinic you volunteer at. Do they do walk-ins."

"For testing, yeah. Tuesday and Thursday afternoons." Sarah put the call on speaker so she could keep highlighting, which was a mistake, because Natalie immediately leaned in. "Why."

"Because I'm fine. That's the thing. I feel completely fine, nothing hurts, nothing's weird, so there's basically no point, right? Like going to the dentist when your teeth don't hurt." Dana's voice had the too-casual rhythm she used when she'd already argued both sides alone in her room for hours. "Plus my mom would see the appointment on the insurance thing. That's a disincentive, honestly. And it's a whole bus ride."

Sarah looked down at the pamphlet Natalie was holding, at the sentence she'd read six times and underlined twice because it kept surprising her. She'd assumed, before the training, that your body told you when something was wrong. Everyone she knew assumed it. The pamphlet said otherwise, flatly, in a paragraph she'd nearly skipped.

"So here's the thing," Sarah said. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms at all. No symptoms. Which means testing is the only reliable way to know if you have one. Feeling fine doesn't prove anything. It just means you feel fine."

There was a silence long enough that Natalie looked up from the pamphlet.

"That's stupid," Dana said finally. "That's a terrible design."

"I know."

"Then how does anyone know?"

"Testing. That's what I just said."

"If I got tested and it was nothing, I'd feel like an idiot for the bus ride alone. And if it wasn't nothing..." She didn't finish. Sarah waited, the way the manual said to wait, letting the silence do work instead of filling it with reassurance she couldn't back up. Behind her, Natalie read the pamphlet's sentence to herself, lips moving, and set it down carefully, flat, like something that had gotten heavier.

"It's Tuesday," Sarah said. "Walk-ins go till five. I could meet you there after my last class. We could get food after, either way. If it's nothing, you're right and you never have to think about it again. And if it's something, it's treatable, and you'd know, and knowing is the whole point." She heard herself assembling it, the practicum voice, and wondered whether Dana could hear the difference between that and her real one.

"Thursday," Dana said. "I need to figure out the insurance thing first. Don't tell anyone."

"I won't."

"I'm serious. Not even your sister."

Natalie raised her eyebrows at the phone. Sarah met her eyes and said, "I won't," and hated how the promise sat, because she'd already decided Natalie would hear it eventually, the way Natalie heard everything, sitting at this table in the light of whatever Sarah was learning first.

Thursday, Sarah stood outside the clinic at four forty with two bus transfers behind her and a text from Dana that said "inside already, don't come in, wait there," which was very like her. Through the window Sarah watched her friend fill out a clipboard in the waiting room, crossing out one line and writing over it, and watched the nurse call a number, and watched Dana stand up too fast, checking her pocket for her phone twice before following the hallway out of sight.

Sarah waited on the steps, holding the pamphlet she'd brought in case Dana wanted to read the sentence herself.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Compound or coating chocolate, which replaces some or all cocoa butter with other fats, sets without tempering but does not have the same snap.
story:
The marble slab had come from the old bakery in Duluth, and it was the coldest thing in Grandmother's kitchen, colder than the tile floor, colder even than the window glass where October was pressing its florid sunset against the pane. Zoey had pulled it from the cupboard herself, because Grandmother was in the chair by the stove with a blanket over her knees, watching, and her hands were not what they had been. The chocolate was in the double boiler, chopped fine, and the thermometer clipped to the pan read 115 degrees and climbing.

"You don't have to watch me," Zoey said. "You could tell me when to stop."

"I'm telling you now. Watch it yourself. That's the whole lesson." Grandmother's voice was dry and light, the way it had been all summer, as if she had decided to ration something. "One fifteen. Take it off."

Zoey had arrived four days ago with a suitcase and a plan she hadn't said out loud: learn the tempering before the fall, before the move to the memory care apartment where there would be no stove she was allowed to use. She had not said this to Grandmother and Grandmother had not said it to her, and the not-saying sat between them like a third person at the table, polite and enormous.

She poured two-thirds of the chocolate onto the slab and began working it with the spatula, spreading and scraping, spreading and scraping, while the mass cooled and thickened and fought her. Her wrist ached. The phone buzzed against the counter and she answered it with her shoulder, still moving the chocolate.

"I'm at the campsite," Priya said. "We're making chocolate-dipped everything, and I bought those candy melts, the little disks? They're already hardening and I didn't do anything to them. No thermometer, nothing. Why did yours take all day?"

"Because mine's real chocolate. Yours is compound chocolate." Zoey scraped the cooling mass back toward the center. "It's got other fats where the cocoa butter should be, some or all of it swapped out, so it sets without tempering." She glanced at Grandmother, who had closed her eyes but was smiling faintly, eavesdropping on the lesson being repeated. "It just doesn't have the same snap."

"Snap?"

"When you break it. It bends instead." Priya said something about nobody at a campsite caring about snap, and Zoey laughed, and then she had to hang up because the chocolate on the slab was at 82 degrees and she needed her whole mind for what came next. She returned the worked chocolate to the warm pan, stirred, watched the thermometer wander up toward 90 and hold there, in the narrow window Grandmother had drawn for her once on a napkin, months ago, like a map of a country that might not exist anymore.

Grandmother had been a baker for forty years, and in the spring she had started asking Zoey the same question twice within an hour, then three times, and Zoey had learned to answer as if for the first time each time, and she had noticed lately that the repetition, which had once made her throat hurt, had begun to desensitize her, and she did not know whether that was mercy or its own small loss. There was a word her English teacher had loved, hermeneutics, the business of interpretation, of reading a text over and over until you understood it or until it changed under your hands. That was what the summer had been. Reading her grandmother and getting different answers.

"Test it," Grandmother said now, without opening her eyes.

Zoey dipped the tip of a knife and let the smear sit thirty seconds. It set dull and streaked. She stared at it, at the bloom ghosting gray across the surface, and felt the specific fury of a person who had done everything right on paper.

"It's not tempered."

"It isn't," Grandmother agreed, and opened her eyes. "You rushed the cooling. You were on the phone."

"I was teaching Priya."

"You were performing teaching." Grandmother pulled the blanket higher. "Do it again."

So she did it again, and it failed again, the fat deciding on some other crystal, some wrong arrangement she couldn't see. The third time she said nothing to anyone, turned the phone face down, and worked the chocolate in a silence so complete she could hear the pilot light. When she tested it, the smear set in fifteen seconds with a shine like wet river stone, and when she broke a corner off the cooled test square it snapped, a clean bright crack, and Grandmother made a small sound, an ah, as if she'd been holding it for an hour.

"There," Grandmother said. "That's it. That's the thing itself."

Zoey dipped strawberries and set them on parchment, and in the morning she would drive the two hours to the new apartment, where the rooms were small and safe and the staff were kind, and bring the box with the ribbon, because Grandmother would want a thing she had made to exist in the place where she could not make things. She was stacking the berries when the phone buzzed again. Priya had sent a picture: campsite, firelight, a dozen lopsided dipped marshmallows, every one of them matte and streak-free and perfectly, unapologetically set. "Nobody cared about snap," the caption said. "They ate them all."

Grandmother was asleep in the chair, mouth open, the blanket rising and falling. Zoey stood at the counter with her glossy strawberries and their beautiful, breakable snap, and broke a test square in half just to hear it again, quietly, so as not to wake her.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
story:
The house was quiet in the way it only got at ten at night, and Sophia spread the score of Mozart's K. 333 across the kitchen table where the light was best. The placement exam was in fourteen hours. Students who passed skipped the first year of theory at the conservatory; students who failed sat in a classroom with sixteen-year-olds learning to spell triads. She had until morning to mark where the exposition ended, where the development began, where the recapitulation brought everything home, and she had promised herself she would do it without the recording first, with only her pencil and her ear from memory.

Her mother drifted through for tea, looked at the score, and said nothing, which was its own kind of language. Sophia sharpened the pencil. The first theme came in the right hand, poised, almost shy, and she bracketed it and wrote A. Sixteen bars later the second theme arrived, singing in a warmer key, and she bracketed that too. The exposition she could feel closing around bar ninety-three, the way a door closes when the hallway light goes off. She drew a double bar line in pencil so light she could erase it if she was wrong.

The trouble started immediately after. The next page was stormier than anything before it, the left hand rolling low, the right hand agitated, and she could not find the seam. It sounded as though Mozart had taken the first theme apart and scattered the pieces, but she could not point to where. She wrote a question mark in the margin and made it through to the recapitulation, unmistakable, the opening tune returning in the original key like a face at a window. So the middle section, whatever it was, lay somewhere in those bars with the question mark.

She was reaching for the recording when she saw the envelope on the counter, addressed to her in her brother's slanted handwriting. Daniel had gone east in August and had written twice since, both letters brief, both read four times. She put the score face down and opened it.

"Dear Soph," it read. "I heard you got the K. 333 for your exam, which is funny, because that was my exam piece, did you know. Third movement though, not the first. I still say the middle section of the first movement is the best part, all that anxiety out of nowhere. Dad keeps asking whether I'll come home for Thanksgiving and I keep saying probably. Tell Mom the probably is real. Love, D."

She read it twice. He had given her a word without knowing it, a word she'd half forgotten from a lecture she'd listened to with one ear: development. That stormy middle, then, the part that had seemed like pure weather, was the development, and it was restless because it broke the exposition's themes into short fragments and moved them quickly through several keys. That was why the ground kept shifting under the tune. That was why she could never find the seam. She sat very still, then put the letter under the fruit bowl where her mother would find it in the morning, or wouldn't, and went back to the table.

Now she listened differently. She played the recording and followed the pencil with her finger, and in the middle of the storm, bar one hundred and six, she heard it: four notes, tucked low in the left hand, that were unmistakably the opening of the first theme. Not the whole tune, just its head, the first few syllables of a sentence spoken inside a gale. She stopped the recording and played the bars at the piano, softly, so as not to wake anyone, and there it was again, in another key entirely, then again somewhere lower, each time shorter, each time further from home. The anxiety in the music wasn't out of nowhere, the way Daniel had said. It was the exposition's own material, fractured and hurried from key to key, and knowing that transmuted the whole passage from chaos into method. She marked the fragments with small brackets, one after another, like tagging birds in flight.

She began to think she understood something larger than Mozart. All year she had been deciding between the conservatory and the state university, and she had been treating the choice as though one path were the tune and the other the storm, one orderly and one a lapse into noise. But the development had taught her that the storm was made of the tune, that the restless middle of anything and its poised beginning were the same material, only broken up and transposed. It was not a comforting thought exactly, because it did not tell her which to choose. It only told her that whichever she chose would contain the other, and that the choice would come round again, in the original key, and she would recognize it when it did.

She worked until one, made judicious marks, erased nothing that mattered. At the top of the middle section she wrote a single word, development, and underlined it once, and beside bar one hundred and six she wrote a smaller note: opening theme lives here too. Then she turned off the lamp and stood in the dark kitchen with her hand still on the score. From the counter the fruit bowl caught a stripe of streetlight through the window, and beneath it, corner of white paper showing, her brother's probably. She left it there and went upstairs.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
Henry would tell anyone who asked that the phone was a want, not a need, and that he had already decided against it. He had been telling himself this for eleven days, which was roughly how long the flat gray box had been sitting in his desk drawer, unopened, purchased with money he had told his father was still in savings. The lying part bothered him less than the arithmetic part. The arithmetic part was becoming an obsession.

The assignment had arrived by email the week before orientation: in three hundred words, explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. The professor called it a diagnostic, not a test, which everyone understood to mean a test. Henry had drafted four versions on the back porch, each one collapsing into jargon halfway through, words like "tightening" and "cooling" stacked on top of each other like furniture in a flooded basement. His younger sister Priya had watched him crumple the fourth attempt and said, "If I can't understand it, you don't either." She was fourteen and merciless and, annoyingly, correct.

On Friday he deposited his paycheck at the bank. He worked at the garden center, hauling mulch, and the pay was unremarkable, but the deposit slip gave him a small, unfamiliar thrill, the kind he usually tried to sublimate into longer runs and fewer text messages. Standing at the counter, he noticed something odd. The teller's screen showed his savings account earning more interest than it had last month. Not dramatically more, but the rate had gone up, recently, and nobody had announced it to him personally, which somehow made it feel more real.

He stood at the counter long enough that the man behind him cleared his throat with theatrical patience. Henry was doing math, but not the kind the teller imagined. The phone cost a definite number. The savings account now paid him a definite, slightly larger number than before for the money he left alone. Leaving it alone had, for the first time in his life, a visible price tag on the other side of it, a small reward for restraint that he could actually watch accrue. He walked home slowly, turning this over.

"And I still don't get what that has to do with inflation," Priya said that evening, from the floor of his room, where she was braiding and unbraiding the same section of her hair. He had attempted an explanation at dinner and their father, who was irascible on his best evenings and this was not his best evening, had said, "At the table we eat," and that had been the end of it.

"Okay," Henry said. "Watch." He pulled the desk chair to the middle of the room like a lecturer. "The central bank raises interest rates. So now the bank pays savers more. Like today, my account, it went up. So people like me, with a paycheck, we start thinking, maybe I move some money I would've spent into savings instead." She rolled her eyes at "people like me," and he pushed on. "So households spend less on stuff. Which means there's less demand for goods out there, all of us wanting to buy things. And when demand for goods drops like that, it helps slow down how fast prices rise. That's the inflation part."

Priya stopped braiding her hair. "Wait. So the government's plan is, make saving more tempting so people stop buying things, and then prices stop climbing because nobody's buying?" He nodded. "That's actually kind of sneaky," she said, with grudging respect. "It doesn't sound like it would work. Like, one person's phone doesn't matter."

"Right, that's what I keep hitting," Henry said. "One person, it's nothing. It only works if everybody does it a little bit. And I can't prove that everyone does. I just know the rates make it more likely." He sat down on the bed. "I think that's the honest version. Rates go up, savers get paid more, households shift some money from spending to saving, demand falls, prices slow. What nobody can tell me is how much, or how fast, or whether it was even the rates that did it." Priya said that sounded like an answer a professor would hate and then secretly like.

Later, with the room dark and the deadline an hour away, Henry opened the desk drawer. The box had a return label he'd printed nine days ago and never used. He typed his three hundred words, and then he sat with his thumb on the phone's power button for a long moment, long enough for the window sticker of the return shipping to matter, and then he set it, still unopened, on the desk beside his laptop and slid the drawer shut on nothing.

In the morning his father found the box at the foot of the stairs with the label taped to the top, and no note. He turned it over once, read the label twice, and carried it out to the car without a word.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The party had moved to the kitchen by ten, where Nadia's mother had left a cake with half its candles already burned down and a punch bowl that tasted mostly of ginger ale and regret. Leah sat on the counter with her phone warm in her pocket, and inside it, unsent, the message she had been drafting for two days. It was for Priya, who had built the data visualization for their economics project, the one they would present on Monday, the one whose y-axis was wrong in a way that made their entire argument look stronger than it was.

She could still see Priya's face on Thursday, when Ms. Okafor had asked if anyone wanted to share a draft. Priya had volunteered so fast, almost before the question finished, and Leah had watched the graph go up on the screen and felt the error land in her chest like a dropped coin. Nobody said anything. Diego definitely saw it; he had checked the same dataset the night before and had grumbled about it in the group chat, in a thread Priya was in, with the observation phrased so indirectly that it read as a compliment. Nice clean numbers, he'd written. Nobody mentioned the obvious mistake, and Leah had understood, in the flattening quiet of that room, that they were all protecting something, though she couldn't have said whether it was Priya or themselves.

At the party, Priya was doing a bad impression of their chemistry teacher, and everyone was laughing, and Leah was laughing too, and the unsent message sat in her phone like a held breath. She had started it three times. The first draft was kind and useless: just a tiny thing, don't worry about it. The second was specific and cruel: your axis makes our conclusion a lie. The third was still open on the screen, cursor blinking after the word Priya.

"You're doing your adjudicating face," Nadia said, appearing with two cups of punch. She handed one over and leaned against the fridge. "Whatever it is, rule against me quickly, I have cake to eat."

"It's the project." Leah turned the phone face down on her knee. "Priya's graph is wrong and nobody's told her and we present Monday."

"So tell her." Nadia said it the way people say jump, as if the hard part were the deciding. But Leah remembered an article her cousin had sent over the summer, something from a business school, about a researcher named Amy Edmondson who had studied hospital teams and found that the best ones reported more mistakes, not fewer, because they weren't actually making more, they were just willing to say so. The article had a phrase for it, the thing a team had to share, the belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. Psychological safety, it was called. She'd liked the phrase at the time the way you like a word you'll never use. Now the graph was wrong, and Diego had gone polite, and Priya was seventeen and wanted to look competent, and Leah was going to have to build that safety herself, alone, over text, before Monday. Or maybe not alone.

Priya was mercurial at parties, loud and then suddenly gone quiet, and Leah never knew which Priya she would get. But the Priya she most wanted to protect was the Thursday one, the one who had raised her hand first. She slid off the counter.

"Hey," she said, arriving at the edge of the circle around Priya's impression. "Can I steal you for a second? Project thing."

Priya followed her into the hallway, where the music dropped to a throb and the somnolence of the late party had started to settle over the kids slumped along the stairs. "Is something broken?"

"The graph isn't. It looks great, honestly, the colors, the labels, all of it. It's just the y-axis. It starts at forty instead of zero, so the drop looks twice as big as it is. It's not your fault, the spreadsheet defaulted that way, Diego's did too." Leah heard herself saying it and thought: this is the draft, the fourth one, happening out loud, unrevisable. "The argument's still right. It's just not that right, and someone will catch it, and it'd be better if it was us."

Priya looked at the wall for a moment. Then at her phone. "Send me the screenshot," she said. "I'll fix it tonight. And text Diego, he should've just said it."

"He was scared of you," Leah said. "We all were a little."

"I'm not scary."

"You're a little scary."

Priya laughed then, the loud version, and pulled up the spreadsheet right there in the hallway, leaning against the banister, thumbing through the numbers while someone's little brother tried to get past them with a plate of cake. "Look," she said, tilting the screen toward Leah, "is that better?"

Leah looked at the new axis starting honestly at zero, at their modest, defensible little line, and shrugged. "It's less impressive," she said.

"Then we say that on Monday," Priya said, and held the phone steady so they could both see.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: To compare leases fairly, add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, such as heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, to get a total monthly cost.
story:
The yellow envelope from the bank had been sitting on the kitchen counter for a week before Maxime opened it, and inside was an appointment card with his name printed in grey ink, a meeting about his first account, which felt official in a way that both exhilarated him and made his stomach tighten. He brought the two leases with him because Camille had texted him that morning: "Bring both papers. We decide today or we lose the June 1st places." The Rue Lapierre lease was 640 a month. The one on Boulevard Rolland was 575. On paper, Rolland was the obvious choice, sixty-five dollars obvious, and Camille had already started calling it "our place."

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and photocopier warmth. Maxime sat in the molded plastic chair by the loan officer's window and spread the two leases side by side on his knees while the queue shuffled forward. He read them more slowly than he had at home, where the paragraphs had slid past him like weather. Here, under fluorescent light with a number ticket going soft in his fist, the words held still. The Lapierre lease said heat and water were included. The Rolland lease said tenant pays all utilities. He looked at the line for a long time, feeling the beginning of something rearranging itself in his head.

Last summer, when he and Camille had talked about moving out of their parents' houses, it had all been hedonistic daydreaming, the fantasy of a fridge they controlled, music at two in the morning, no father turning off the hallway light. Camille had spun visions of house parties the way other people planned careers. Maxime had gone along with it because going along was easier than saying he was afraid, and because the fantasy was genuinely sweet. He remembered them lying on the hood of her brother's car in July, naming the streets they would live on, and how certain it had all seemed, and how neither of them had once said the word budget.

Now his number was called, and he stepped up to the teller window with the papers still in his hand. The teller, a woman named Doris according to her nameplate, glanced at the leases when he set them down beside his banking card. "You're moving out?" she asked, counting his deposit. He said maybe, that he and his friend were comparing two apartments. "My nephew did that last year," she said. "He learned the hard way. To compare leases fairly, you add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, like heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, and that total monthly cost tells you which place is actually cheaper." She slid his receipt under the glass. "Cheaper rent isn't always the cheaper place."

He sat back down on the plastic chair and did it. On the back of the appointment card, in handwriting that got smaller as the space ran out, he listed what Rollland would cost on top of its 575: electricity for a drafty third floor, heat through a Quebec winter, water, internet, tenant insurance because the lease required it. He estimated honestly, using his mother's old bills, which he had looked up that morning without knowing why. The total came out above 790. Then he did Lapierre: 640 with heat and water included, plus electricity, internet and insurance. It came in under 720. He added the column twice, because the arithmetic seemed to be telling him something he didn't want it to tell him.

He texted Camille a photograph of the card with its cramped figures, then typed: "Rolland costs more every month once you count everything. Lapierre is actually the cheaper place." He watched the three dots appear and disappear twice. When her reply came, it was longer than he expected: "I ran my own numbers and you're right. My dad said the same thing years ago and I thought he was just being negative. It feels like an acquittal for him, honestly. Fine. Lapierre. But Maxime, I'm grieving the cheap fantasy a little." He read it three times, sitting there in the bank's warm hum, and felt the strange double weight of having won the argument and lost something glittering that they would never get back.

He walked out into the parking lot holding the card with the numbers on one side and his appointment time on the other. There was still a gap he couldn't close: the estimates were estimates, and he had no way of knowing whether the electricity on Rolland's third floor was forty dollars or ninety, whether his mother's old bills meant anything for a different building. He was choosing on arithmetic built out of guesses, and he knew it, and he also knew it was still better than choosing on rent alone. He got in the car and texted Camille back.

"Sign Lapierre before someone else does."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, but individual workers in industries that now face cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or wages.
story:
Jacob spread his flashcards across the kitchen table the way his teacher had shown them, one column for Portugal, one for England, the old Ricardo example flattened onto index cards. The presentation was first period tomorrow, ten minutes on comparative advantage, and he had the logic down cold: even if one country made both goods better, both could still gain from trade, because each should make the thing it gave up least to make. He could recite it in his sleep. What he could not do, yet, was make anyone care.

His mother was at the sink, rinsing strawberries for Grandpa's visit. "He's coming at four," she said, "and he's in one of his moods, so don't start on economics with him."

"Why would I start on anything with him?"

"Because you start on everything with everyone." She set the colander down. "Just remember his plant closed in '09. He has opinions."

Grandpa arrived with the newspaper folded under his arm and the smell of pipe smoke still in his jacket even though he'd quit years ago. He ate the strawberries slowly, watching Jacob shuffle cards. "Schoolwork?" he asked finally.

"Presentation. Trade. It's actually kind of beautiful," Jacob said, before he could stop himself. "Comparative advantage. Two countries trade and both of them get richer. Total income goes up. Everybody wins."

Grandpa set his fork down with a click that Jacob felt in his teeth. There was a silence in which he had a presentiment of having stepped somewhere he couldn't step back from.

"Everybody," Grandpa said. "The plant on Fell Street made forty years of whoever bought whatever we shipped out. Richer. And then the imports came in cheaper, and I trained my replacement without knowing it, me and four hundred other men, and the town's still trying to resuscitate itself with antique shops and a farmers market. So tell me who won, college boy."

Jacob's mouth opened to deliver the rebuttal he'd rehearsed, the one about efficiency and totals, and nothing came out. Because the two ideas were both in the room at once and neither would dissolve into the other. He looked at his cards, at the neat columns, and the columns suddenly looked like they were hiding something rather than showing it.

"Wait," he said. He pulled a napkin from the holder and turned it over. "Okay. The country. The whole country's income goes up. That part's true, that's what I learned. But you're saying that doesn't reach everybody in it." He drew a box around the columns. "You lost your job. Wages, jobs, the people making the thing that's now cheaper coming in. That can still happen even while the total goes up."

"So it raises the money and cuts the men," Grandpa said.

"It can, yeah. Both at the same time. That's what I'm seeing." Jacob stared at the napkin. "That's actually worse in a way. Because if it made the whole country poorer, somebody would notice. If it makes it richer, the numbers look fine."

Grandpa leaned back. His shoulders had come down from around his ears, though his eyes hadn't softened. "Your grandmother wanted me to take the retraining offer. Computers, down at the community college. I was fifty-one and I'd been running a lathe since I was twenty-two, and I told her no man my age learns a new trade. Some nights I think I was right and some nights I know I was stubborn, and I've stopped trying to decide which."

The kitchen clock ticked toward five. His mother came in with tea, set a cup in front of each of them, and retreated without a word, which was her way of saying she wanted to hear the rest.

"So what do I say tomorrow?" Jacob asked. "I've got ten minutes."

"You say the true thing and the hard thing," Grandpa said. "The country gains. Say it. Then say who paid for it, and say you don't have the answer to that, because you don't and neither does your teacher."

Jacob sat up past eleven, redoing the slides. He cut the part where he'd called it beautiful. He added a slide with just two sentences, no clip art: that trade on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, and that workers in the industries facing cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or their wages, both true at once. He wrote a final slide with a picture he'd taken that afternoon on his phone, the Fell Street plant from the bus, its windows boarded, a banner across the front advertising loft apartments coming soon. He couldn't decide if the banner was hopeful or bellicose, a declaration of war on what the building had been, and he left the slide without a caption.

At breakfast his mother asked if he was ready.

"I don't know if it's a presentation anymore," he said. "It might be an argument with myself in front of twenty-six people."

"That's called being honest," she said, and handed him his lunch.

He slung his bag over his shoulder, napkin still folded in his pocket with the box drawn around the columns, and went out into the gray morning to say both true things.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
Annabelle found the cuff in the bathroom cabinet behind her mother's hairspray, still in its plastic sleeve, a gift from an aunt who gave everyone practical presents and then never mentioned them again. Her health teacher had assigned each student a family member to monitor for a week, and since her mother refused on principle and her brother was twelve and bounced off walls, Annabelle had written her grandfather's name on the form without asking him first. He lived four blocks away, close enough that she could ride her bike over after school, which she did now with the cuff jammed in her backpack next to a banana she was already regretting.

Grandpa Ray was in the backyard on his knees in the tomato bed when she arrived, and he didn't look up right away because he was arguing with a squirrel. "You've got the whole oak," he told it. "The whole oak, and you want my Romas." He was seventy-one and built like a fence post, and Annabelle had never once seen him sick, not a cough, not a day in bed, and she said so as she propped her bike against the shed. He accepted this as plain fact rather than flattery, the way he accepted weather.

"You want my blood pressure," he said, when she explained the assignment, reading the numbers, writing them down, learning to say what they meant. "For school." He wiped his hands on his jeans and squinted at her. "I feel fine, so it must be fine. That's how a body works. When something's wrong, it tells you."

Annabelle had read the opposite the night before, in the packet Mr. Okoye had handed out, a paragraph she'd had to read twice because it seemed almost like a trick. She hadn't said anything about it yet, though, because she wanted to see the numbers first. "Can we just measure it anyway?" she asked. "That's the whole assignment. You just sit there."

He let her wrap the cuff around his arm, which was tanned and corded and smelled faintly of tomato leaves, and he sat very still in the lawn chair with the expression of a man being photographed for a passport. The machine whirred, tightened, and thought. Annabelle watched the screen, then looked again, then looked at her own handwriting when she'd copied the numbers down, because the top number was 158 and her notes said anything over 140 for that number counted as high. "It's high," she said.

"It can't be," Grandpa Ray said. "I'd know."

"That's the thing," Annabelle said. She unfolded the packet, found the paragraph, and read it aloud to the yard, to the squirrel, to him. "High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all. That's why they call it a silent killer. It gets found mainly by measuring it." She looked up. "That's the actual phrase. Silent killer. So feeling fine doesn't really tell you anything."

He was quiet for a moment, which for him was a long time, because he was not a quiet man; at Thanksgiving he turned positively bellicose about politics and had to be given a second helping of pie as a diversion. "Well," he said finally. "That's a dirty trick of the body. A man should get some warning." He flexed his arm where the cuff had been, as if he could externalize the whole thing, push it out through his skin and be done with it. "Your grandmother's machine is in the hall closet. I never used it. She used to nag me about it and I used to tell her I felt fine."

Annabelle measured him again the next day, and the day after, and on Thursday she sat at his kitchen table graphing the numbers while he cooked, refusing his offer of sausage and making them both salmon instead, because the packet said diet changed the reading and she wanted to see if that was true and how fast. He ate it without complaint but with commentary. "You're turning my kitchen into a lab," he said. "Next you'll be checking my genotype, telling me what I'm doomed to." She told him that wasn't how it worked, mostly, and he waved the spatula at her in a way that meant he loved her and would not be told.

The truth was she liked the riding over, the graphing, the sense that the numbers were a language she was slowly becoming fluent in. It also complicated things. On Friday the top number was down to 146, and she didn't know whether to credit the fish, the walks he'd grudgingly started taking with her around the block, or plain daily variation, and her notes had an honest column headed "can't tell." Some things the packet promised were simple and turned out to have edges you couldn't see.

That night her mother called from the kitchen, phone pressed to her ear, and handed it over with a strange expression. "It's for you. It's Grandpa." Annabelle took it, expecting a complaint about the salmon.

Instead he read her a letter. He'd written it that afternoon, he said, and he wanted her to hear it before he mailed it to her teacher, because he didn't fully trust the internet and the letter was more real. "Dear Mr. Okoye," it began. "You assigned my granddaughter to check my blood pressure and I want you to know I thought this was an intrusion at first. I have felt fine for seventy-one years and I assumed that settled the matter. Your packet says high blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, and is found mainly by measuring it, and I have thought about that every day this week. I did not know the machine in my hall closet could tell me something my own body would not. I am walking now with Annabelle in the evenings. I would not have agreed to this for a doctor. Tell your students old men will listen to a granddaughter when they will not listen to anyone else." There was more, something about her grandmother, whose nagging he now understood had been love wearing an annoying hat, but his voice caught and he skipped ahead. "So that's the letter," he said. "Should I mail it?"

Annabelle stood in the kitchen holding the phone, the graph in her backpack upstairs, the honest column still unfinished, everything she knew and everything she couldn't tell yet balanced against the seventy-one years of feeling fine. "Yes," she said. "Mail it. And bring tomatoes tomorrow, we're out."

"I'll bring the ugly ones," he said. "The squirrel can have first pick of the rest."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The drama room smelled of dust and old paint, and Alexander stood at the center of it holding a pencil that he had already chewed to splinters. Mr. Ruiz had given the one-acts to the seniors and the one act to him, a junior, because his prompt book for the fall show had been meticulous, and now that trust sat in his hands like something warm he was afraid of dropping. The play was ten minutes long, two characters, a bench, a lamppost. The rehearsal was his to run.

He had blocked the whole thing at his kitchen table the night before, drawing arrows in green ink, and the arrows made a kind of sense on paper that they refused to make on the floor. Priya, who played the sister, kept drifting toward the back wall whenever her character was upset, and from the third row of folding chairs, where Alexander sat, she disappeared into shadow and became a voice without a body.

"Come down," he called, and then, because that sounded like something a director on a television show would say, "I mean, toward me."
