"Isn't the front called down?" Priya asked. She hadn't done theatre before. "That seems backwards. Down should be the important place. Up is winning."

"I don't know," Alexander said, which cost him something to admit, because he had assumed all year that the vocabulary was the easy part, the part you memorized and never questioned. He had a thespian friend at the community theatre across town, Marcus, who owed him a favor for repairing the lights during their summer production, and he texted him between scenes: why is the back of a stage called up. Marcus wrote back before Alexander had finished reblocking the lamppost argument: because the old stages were raked, they sloped down toward the audience. So upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it. Alexander read it twice. The words stopped being arbitrary and became a fossil of some older architecture, and he felt the small, private pleasure of a thing snapping into place, though it also meant his green arrows had been drawn in a vocabulary he had never actually understood.

At the next rehearsal he tested it. He moved Priya downstage during the confession, three steps toward the folding chairs, and her whole face arrived in the light, and the moment worked so well it startled her. He tried the countermove too, pushing Devon, who played the brother, upstage for the lie, letting him retreat into the flat gray distance where lies apparently belonged. He could not have said whether the blocking was honest or merely effective. Marcus's fact gave him directions, not reasons, and the difference between those two things kept him up that night more than he wanted to admit.

The shows had a budget, a modest disbursement from the student activities fund that Mr. Ruiz let Alexander manage himself, and he learned that directing was partly arithmetic: twelve dollars for a replacement lamp, eight for paint, a decision about whether the bench could be borrowed from the choir room without a form. He was careful with it, almost miserly, and Priya teased him about counting quarters while she recuperated between scenes, draped over the bench with a cold pack on her knee she had twisted in gym class, insisting she would be fine by Friday. He let her rest because the alternative was a scene without its center, and resting looked, from the third row, like an actor doing nothing, which was another thing he had never known: stillness had to be built, allowed for, budgeted like anything else.

On the night of the performance the raked-stage fact returned to him in the wings. Marcus had come, sitting somewhere in the middle, and afterward he found Alexander by the snacks and said the blocking was clean, that the upstage retreat at the climax was the best choice in the piece. Alexander wanted to explain that the choice had been half accident, half an actor's twisted knee and a borrowed bench, and that he still wasn't sure whether he had directed the play or merely watched it assemble itself out of favors, injuries, and one text message. Instead he said thank you, because directors probably said thank you.

Mr. Ruiz asked him to assistant-direct the spring musical, which was the thing he had wanted since September, and Alexander said yes before he had thought it through, and felt the shape of the next three months close over him like water: the gains and the losses all mixed together, alluvial, deposited in him by a current he had only partly steered. He would give up the track season for it. He already knew that, and he already knew he would do it anyway, and that these two facts could both be true at once was something no direction, up or down, seemed to resolve.

Afterward, alone, he stacked the folding chairs against the wall and then rolled the bench back to its mark, center stage, a little up of true center. He looked at it from the back row, then from the wings, then from downstage, where the light still burned because nobody had switched it off, and he stood there a moment longer in the slope of it, facing out toward all those empty seats.

He switched off the light and took the bench home.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
Paige unearthed her economics notes from the bottom of her backpack the way an archaeologist might exhume a burial, layer by layer, one crumpled handout at a time. On Saturday she was supposed to explain, to a mock-interview panel her mother had arranged for a college scholarship, how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had a paragraph memorized. The problem was that when her mother had asked her over dinner to say it in plain words, the paragraph had dissolved the moment it left her mouth, and her younger brother Theo had laughed so hard he knocked over his milk.

On Thursday afternoon she was still at the kitchen table, flashcards fanned out like a losing hand, when Theo and his friend Marcus burst in arguing. They ran a lemonade stand at the curb, and the argument was about the price. Marcus wanted to raise it from a dollar to a dollar twenty-five, starting tomorrow. "Cups and sugar are going to cost more next month," he said. "Everything's going up. If we wait, we lose money." Theo said that was a rip-off, and Marcus said it wasn't a rip-off, it was planning ahead.

Paige started to shoo them toward the porch, then stopped. "Marcus, why do you think cups will cost more?" "Because everything's getting more expensive. My dad says so. Everybody says so." "So you're raising your price before anything actually costs more." Marcus shrugged, as if the distinction were trivial, which in a way it was, and in a way it was everything. "If you knew for sure," she asked, "that cups and sugar would stay the same price all summer, would you still charge a dollar twenty-five?" He thought about it, chewing the inside of his cheek. "I guess not. A dollar's easier. Nobody haggles at a dollar."

She sat back down at the table, not looking at the boys, and pulled one flashcard from the pile. It said, in her own handwriting, that if people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down. She had copied it from the textbook without once picturing anyone doing it. Now she could picture Marcus, ten years old, raising his lemonade price twenty-five cents purely because he expected everything else to cost more next month, and she could see the whole thing running in reverse. It was like being handed a completed puzzle and realizing you'd had all the pieces all along.

"Theo," she said, "what's a disincentive?" "A thing that stops you from doing something." "Right. So if the stand charges too much, that's a disincentive for people to buy. But if people trust the stand to keep the price at a dollar, they don't brace for it to jump. They just come and buy." Theo looked at her for a moment and said, "So the price stays low because nobody expects it to go up." It was almost embarrassingly trenchant, and Paige told him so, which he took as an insult until she explained it wasn't.

"But how does the bank raising interest rates make people trust it?" Marcus asked, and here Paige faltered, because that was the part she still couldn't say cleanly. "I think," she said slowly, "that's the part where it gets expensive to borrow, so people buy less, and that cools things off. But honestly, I'm not sure I could prove the connection between that and what you two were arguing about. I know the expectation matters. I know people trusting the bank keeps prices down. The middle part I'm still shaky on." Her mother, chopping peppers at the counter, said that admitting the shaky part might be the most convincing thing she could say to a panel. Paige wrote at the bottom of the card, "say what I don't know," which felt like either wisdom or surrender.

Saturday morning, before her mother drove her to the interview, Paige walked the three houses to the curb stand to buy a goodbye lemonade. A new sign hung from the table, written in Theo's stubborn capital letters: OUR PRICE IS ONE DOLLAR ALL SUMMER. TRUST US. Marcus was taking a stack of bills from a neighbor lady who said she'd buy a cup every morning now that she knew the price would hold. Paige felt something in her chest loosen, a small step, nothing more, but a step.

She was halfway down the driveway, cards in her back pocket, when Theo jogged up beside her. "We sold out twice," he said. "So Marcus had an idea." He held up a paper cup that was, unmistakably, an inch shorter than the one from yesterday, still priced at one dollar, under the sign that said TRUST US. "Don't tell Mom," he said. "We call it the new size."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The laminated menu had a coffee ring on it, and Maya kept smoothing the article over the ring as if the words underneath would flatten out and behave. The article was in Turkish, one column from that morning's paper, about a youth orchestra in Izmir that had lost its rehearsal space and would give a single free concert in a park before the instruments went into storage. In ninety minutes her cousin Efe was calling from Istanbul, and she had promised, in her careful handwritten Turkish, that she would tell him what the article said. Out loud. No English. Her mother called it a promise; Maya privately called it a dare.

She was sitting in the back booth of Deniz's family restaurant because home had too many softer places to give up, and a restaurant, with its clatter and its obligation to order something, kept her honest. Deniz, who was seventeen and had opinions about everything, was wiping down the table across the aisle and watching Maya drag her finger along the first line for what had to be the fourth time.

"You're doing the word-by-word thing," Deniz said. She said it the way other people said you forgot your umbrella, mildly, without malice, maybe with a small amount of entertainment.

Maya looked up. "It's a short article."

"You've been on the same paragraph since I refilled your water."

"I don't know all the words."

"Which ones do you need?"

The question sat there, and Maya realized she had never actually asked herself that. She needed enough to summarize it aloud. That was the assignment Efe had set when she'd asked him, over a crackling video call, to help her stop translating in her head. One article a week, he'd said, tell me what it says. Not every word. What it says.

"There's a concert," she said slowly, reading the headline again. "In a park. But I don't know when. The date's in there somewhere, I think, but the middle is all this stuff about the director and his feelings about the municipality, and there's this long quote that honestly feels gratuitous, like the reporter just liked the sound of it."

Deniz came over and set the water pitcher down on the corner of the table, out of Maya's territory but within her own reach, a negotiation of space they had worked out months ago. "Okay. Do you need the director's feelings?"

"For a summary? Probably the fact that they exist, not what they are."

"Then don't read the middle. What you're doing, going word by word when you only need the date, that's the expensive way. Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea. Scanning means searching the text for one specific detail, like a name or a number." She plucked the pen from behind Maya's ear, which was gratuitous in its own right, and tapped the third paragraph. "So scan for this one. Look for numbers, not words."

Maya bent over the page. Her eye, obedient for once, went hunting for shapes, for digits, for the little numeral with its tail, and there it was, third line from the bottom, a date, and beside it a time she had missed completely on all four of her slow passes. She felt something loosen in her chest, the same feeling as when a locker combination turns over on the last number.

"Twenty-third," she said. "It's on the twenty-third. I read that whole paragraph twice and the date just sat there."

"The date was always winning," Deniz said. "You were just running the wrong race." She went back to the aisle with the rag, and Maya sat with the strange arithmetic of it: she had spent twenty minutes she could have spent on the whole task, because she'd assumed that reading meant reading everything, in order, at the same speed. Was that a belief she'd internalized somewhere, back in some classroom where slowness counted as virtue? She genuinely didn't know. Maybe skimming was a skill for later, when you had enough of the language to catch yourself when you slipped. Or maybe this was how you got enough of the language. Both felt possible, which was uncomfortable, and she noted the discomfort the way she noted a word she didn't know, carefully, in the margin.

She tried the skim next, letting her eyes move in quick diagonal passes over the whole column, grabbing what they could. Names surfaced: the director, the mayor, a girl who played the cello and was quoted once, mercifully briefly. Numbers: the date, the time, the number of students in the orchestra. She filled the margin of the page with her own shorthand, and then, on a fresh napkin, she began building the summary. Efe had taught her to work from the lemma, the dictionary form of a verb, and then bend it into whatever tense she needed, and so she wrote konser, park, öğrenci, and then verbs in their naked infinitives like a scaffolding she could hang sentences on.

At the small table by the window, an older couple finished their meal, and the husband counted out coins with a trembling precision, and Maya watched him without meaning to and thought about how his hands were scanning, sorting for one specific coin among many. Then the phone buzzed. Efe.

She answered in Turkish, and the first sentence came out crooked, and Efe, bless him, did not correct it, only waited. She told him about the orchestra, the lost rehearsal space, the park, the twenty-third. She left out the director's feelings. When she stumbled on the word for "free" he gave it to her once, quietly, and she said it back and felt it begin to settle somewhere.

Efe asked a question she hadn't prepared for, whether she thought the city should have helped them, and Maya said she didn't know yet, that the article hadn't really said, that maybe she'd find a second article, and Deniz, wiping the table across the aisle, mouthed the word "scanning" at her and grinned.

Maya folded the napkin along its creases, the summary inside like a small clean parcel, and held it up toward the aisle. "Another one," she said, in Turkish, and pointed at the paper on the counter.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
Jordan had been sitting in the plastic chair outside Room 4 for eleven minutes, rehearsing what he would say, when the door opened and a nurse called his name.

The plan had started three weeks earlier, in Mr. Okafor's health class, when the sign-up sheet for the teen clinic volunteer program went around. Jordan had written his name mostly to prove something to Priya Raman, who had claimed, with the cheerful certainty he found unbearable, that he avoided anything requiring him to talk about bodies out loud. Now he was committed to shadowing Dr. Alvarez one afternoon a week, and his job today was to practice explaining the clinic's services to a standardized patient, an actor hired to play a nervous teenager named Sam.

"Sam's coming in with a question about testing," Dr. Alvarez said, gesturing him into the exam room. "You take it. I'll be at the desk." She sat down and became, apparently, furniture.

The actor was a college student named Deshawn, maybe twenty, with a laminated card of patient details folded in his hand. He slouched onto the table in a hoodie and looked at the floor. "So," he said. "Hypothetically. How does somebody even get tested here?"

Jordan's rehearsed sentences dissolved. He got out the basics in pieces: you could walk in, you didn't need a parent's permission in this state, the tests were quick, and if anything came back positive most infections were treatable. "Do you want the pamphlet with the clinic hours?" he asked, and Deshawn took it, which felt like a small victory.

"Okay, but the hypothetical person," Deshawn said, turning the pamphlet over. "Say he was with somebody and things got weird. Like they started, and then he wanted to stop, and the other person said they already agreed so it doesn't count. Does the agreement, like, lock in?"

Jordan's first instinct was to hedge, to externalize the answer onto some authority, to say he'd ask Dr. Alvarez. But she was right there pretending to chart something, and the question sat in the room, plainly his. He thought about the condom demonstration he'd practiced on a wooden model two sessions ago, about contraception being something you plan before, not after. Consent, he realized, worked differently. It wasn't a one-time payment. "No," he said. "It doesn't lock in. Consent has to be freely given, and you can withdraw it at any time. Even after things have already started."

Deshawn looked up at him for the first time. "Even in the middle?"

"Even in the middle. That's the rule."

"So the hypothetical person could just say stop."

"That's the whole point of saying stop," Jordan said, and heard, as he said it, that he believed it.

They ran through the scenario twice more, Deshawn escalating the complications each time: what if the other person got angry, what if they'd been drinking, what if the hypothetical person had said yes a hundred times before. Jordan answered some cleanly and fumbled others, and on the fumbles he made himself say "I don't actually know, but here's who would" and slid the clinic's after-hours card across the desk. He had always distrusted people who admitted ignorance so readily, had privately filed it under weakness, a profligate spending of credibility he couldn't afford. Watching Deshawn relax each time he said it, he began to suspect the opposite: that certainty hoarded too tightly curdled into something useless.

Afterward, in the hallway, Dr. Alvarez stood up from being furniture. "You told him he could change his mind," she said.

"That was the right answer, wasn't it?" Jordan asked, and heard how much he needed it to be.

"It was the right answer. What you didn't know was whether to say it like you meant it. You figured that out around the second time." She checked her watch. "Same time next week. Priya's on the schedule, so be ready to watch her be better at the empathy part than you."

"She's not better at everything."

"She's better at the part you're worst at, which is the one you notice. That's just hierarchy, Jordan. Doesn't mean anyone's winning." She said it lightly, but he recognized the shape of it, the way a single ranking could quietly become a hegemony in his head, governing how he saw every room he walked into.

He took the bus home with the after-hours card still in his pocket, and somewhere around the fourth stop he pulled out his phone and texted Priya: next week you're on with the actors, I'll watch how you do the listening part. He typed and deleted three attempts at a joke about it, and finally sent the plain version, and put the phone face-down on his knee as the buildings went by.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
The comp sci room smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Sarah had forty minutes to make her BankAccount class work before Mr. Rowley collected the unit. She had three fields, balance and owner and accountNumber, all mercifully private. What she did not have was a getter for balance that passed a single test, because the test did not compile, because the test had been written before the class existed.

"Mr. Rowley," she said, "the test file can't even run. There's nothing to test yet."

"That's the point." He was a dour man who assigned work like verdicts and never softened a deadline. "Kent Beck made a whole method of it. You write the failing test first."

Her partner, Devon, leaned across the aisle. "He means it's red, green, refactor. That's the cycle. Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code."

"Why would I prove I failed on purpose?"

"Because the failure is information," Devon said, and went back to his screen, which was black except for a red bar.

Sarah looked at her own monitor, where the compiler had underlined getBalance in furious red. It was a strange pedagogy, this business of trying to inculcate discipline through deliberate error, like teaching someone to swim by shoving them in and grading the splash. But the red underline was not vague. It named exactly what did not exist, and that was more than her usual method offered, which was writing two hundred lines and hoping.

So she built the class around the test instead of the other way around. She typed the private fields, then the getter, one method, six lines. She ran the test. The bar went green so suddenly that she flinched, as if she'd gotten away with something. Then came the part Devon called refactor, and she understood it only when she saw her own mess: two constructors doing the same work, a validation check repeated in three places. She cleaned up the code while the bar stayed green, running the test after each small change, the way you keep a hand on the wall in the dark.

At the next desk, Marcus was doing what she used to do, writing the whole class first, no tests, and now his output was a wall of nulls. "It worked yesterday," he kept saying.

"Write one test," Sarah said. "Just one."

"For what?"

"For whatever you think works. If it passes, you know that part's fine."

He wrote a test for the deposit method. It failed. He stared at it, then at his deposit code, then said, almost wonderingly, "I never add to the balance. I reassign it." He fixed one line and the bar went green, and he sat back like a man who had been shown a trapdoor in his own house.

By the end of the period Sarah had a class she trusted and a feeling she did not entirely trust. The cycle felt less like a rule than a vernacular, a shared way of speaking about code that she had started to think in without deciding to. What she could not settle was whether the tests proved her program right or only proved it matched her expectations, which were exactly the thing most likely to be wrong. She had written the tests, so she had chosen the questions. She raised her hand.

"Question," she said. "If I write the test first, aren't I just grading my own exam?"

Mr. Rowley almost smiled. "Write a test you expect to fail," he said, "and see what it tells you."

She turned back to the keyboard and typed a withdrawal for more than the balance, watching the cursor blink at the end of the line.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
story:
Eric had forty minutes before his next round, and he was hiding in the back hallway of the science wing with a laptop and a problem. The problem was that his debate coach, Ms. Okafor, had signed him up for something called Creative Interpretation, a pilot event at this tournament where instead of arguing about the resolution you wrote and staged a ten-minute play about a moment from your own life. Eric had never written a play. He had written cases, blocks, and one truly grim poem in seventh grade. He had until the end of the day.

He had chosen his moment already, which was the easy part: last spring, in the hospital waiting room, when his grandfather's surgery ran long and Eric's mother had taught him gin rummy on the seat of her coat to keep them both from unraveling. What he could not figure out was how a page told people what to do. In a debate case, everything was spoken. You just said the words. But a play seemed to require bodies, a table, a deck of cards, and he had no idea how you wrote any of that down.

His round before lunch had been against a girl from Ravenswood who ran a case about determinism, the idea that every choice was already fixed by what came before it, so that punishment could never be deserved, only administered. Eric had won on a technicality, which felt like losing slowly. Now, typing "MOM shuffles the deck" and then not knowing what to do with it, he thought about her case anyway. If everything was already written, then this play was written too, and he was just the last one to find out.

That was when Priya found him. Priya was his partner in policy debate, and she had lost her own round and was carrying two slices of pizza balanced on a napkin like a peace offering. "Ms. Okafor said you're doing the play thing," she said, sitting down beside him on the floor. "That's hilarious. You analyze everything. You'll try to argue with your own characters." He took a slice. He did not argue with this, because it was true.

She read over his shoulder, which he usually hated, and pointed at the screen. "Why are those lines in parentheses?" He had put "(MOM shuffles the deck. ERIC watches the door.)" in parentheses mostly because it looked wrong sitting naked on the page. "Honestly, because it looked wrong," he said. Priya's older brother did community theatre, and she squinted at the screen for a second and then started laughing, which he took personally until she explained. "My brother did this at his first read-through. The script had directions in italics, and this one actor, this guy Dale, just read them out loud. Whole room sitting in a circle, and Dale goes, 'Tom exits quietly,' in a completely normal voice. Because Dale hadn't figured out that stage directions are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines." She wiped her eyes. "The director still says 'Tom exits quietly' to him in the lobby. It's like their hello."

Eric looked at his parentheses. The page had been talking to two different audiences the whole time, and he had only known about one of them. Everything in parentheses was an instruction, a quiet conversation with whoever staged the thing, and everything else was what the room would actually hear. He felt the particular vertigo of a rule that had always existed becoming visible. He began writing in earnest, directions in parentheses, dialogue bare, and Priya read both as he typed, doing the mom in a low voice and the Eric character in a voice that was annoyingly accurate.

The twist came at the staging itself, which happened in an empty chemistry classroom with three chairs and a volunteer. Ms. Okafor had recruited the Ravenswood girl, whose name was Dara, to read the mother, on the theory that opponents make the best scene partners. Dara read beautifully, and when she reached the line "(MOM shuffles the deck)," she paused, and Eric held his breath, and she did not read it aloud. She looked up at him over the page. "Parentheses," she said. "I know." Then she mimed shuffling, and Priya, in the back, whispered "Tom exits quietly" and had to leave the room about her incipient laughter.

Afterward, walking out, Eric tried to amortize the day against some ledger of what it had cost him, the lost rounds, the ruined Saturday, and found the accounting refused to work, because he had gotten something that would not divide into hours. Dara caught up with him near the buses. "Your mom teaching you cards to keep from crying," she said. "That's not really determinism, you know. She chose that." Eric said, "Maybe. I'm still not sure what's fixed and what isn't." Dara shrugged and held out the script pages, warm from her hand. "Then leave it in parentheses."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
story:
The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of dust and old hymnals, and Faith had the place to herself for two hours every Thursday because Mrs. Okafor trusted her with the key. She spread the score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C minor across the organ bench and took out a pencil. Her college audition was in eleven weeks, and the written theory exam would ask her to mark the form of a movement: exposition, development, recapitulation. She had decided, with the private stubbornness she reserved for plans nobody else knew about, that she would learn to do it before anyone could teach it to her.

She had taught herself other things this way. Two summers ago she had learned to rebuild a bicycle wheel from a library book, alone in her grandfather's garage, because he had refused to do it for her and equally refused to watch her fail at it. He had sat inside with the radio on, an epicure of silence and coffee, and when she wheeled the finished bike past the window he had only nodded. She thought of that nod more often than she thought of anything he actually said. He had died in March, and the scholarship folder he never got to see was folded into her backpack right now, under the score.

She began at the beginning, pencil hovering. The first theme announced itself in C minor, stern and compact, and she bracketed it with a light stroke. She remembered her teacher's offhand remark from last month, that in a minor-key sonata the second theme usually goes to the dominant. That had seemed reasonable enough to repeat. So when the music slid out of its stormy opening into something warmer, she wrote G major in the margin and felt the small satisfaction of a fact confirmed.

Then she played the passage again, because the harmony under her fingers did not feel like G major at all. It felt broader, rounder, three flats' worth of calm. She counted the key signature on the page. E-flat major. She sat back on the bench and stared at the two words she had written, then crossed out G major with a single line.

"That's not what you said," she said aloud, to the empty room, to the photograph of the choir from 1974 on the wall. She got out her phone and searched, expecting a correction somewhere, an exception she could file and forget. Instead she found the opposite. In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major. E-flat major in a movement in C minor. She read it three times, and each reading made her earlier certainty look more like a guess that had happened to sound confident.

She felt the familiar heat in her ears, the one she got when a wrong note carried her name on it. In ninth grade she had told the whole orchestra that the bridge passage was in the dominant, had argued it, and had been wrong in front of forty chairs of raised bows. Her teacher had let her argue for a full minute before correcting her, and Faith had never decided whether that had been cruelty or a gift. She had stopped volunteering answers for a year. Now she wondered whether the safer habit had cost her more than the embarrassment had.

Her little brother, Dev, knocked on the choir room door with twenty minutes left in her slot, holding the violin case he pretended to resent carrying. "Mom's outside," he said. "She's being penurious about the parking meter, so you have like a minute." He leaned over the score while she gathered her pencil and eraser. "What's all the bracketing?"

"Sonata form. First theme, second theme, all of it." She pointed at her crossed-out margin note. "I thought the second theme went to the dominant. It doesn't. In a minor key it goes to the relative major. E-flat, here." Dev nodded the way he nodded at everything she said about music, half belief and half deference, and she was suddenly careful not to enjoy the deference. That was the thing about being the one who explained: you could be wrong with an audience.

"Is that bad, that you were wrong?" he asked.

"It's bad if I don't find it." She slid the score into her bag, then took it out again and opened it flat on the bench, unwilling to close it mid-thought. She played the exposition once more at quarter speed, her left hand only, listening for the exact measure where the key turned, and drew a firm double bar where the exposition ended. Somewhere after that the development would take these themes apart, and later the recapitulation would gather them home, but she had eleven weeks, and tonight she had one honest boundary line and one corrected word.

Dev waited in the doorway, tapping his bow against his leg. "Faith. Minute."

She zipped the bag, turned off the lamp above the bench, and pocketed Mrs. Okafor's key. In the vestibule, past the baptismal font, she stopped with her hand on the heavy door. "Tomorrow you're my audience," she said. "Bring the violin."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million.
story:
The assignment was due at eight the next morning, and Laura had brought it to the beach anyway, which her brother called insane and she called efficient, since the graph was on her phone and the ocean was free. She sat on the folded towel with her back to the dunes and opened the picture her teacher had posted: a jagged line climbing upward across a hundred years, sawtoothed, relentless. The instructions said to find how much carbon dioxide had risen since measurements began. The line started somewhere on the left edge, at a value the picture did not label, and the whole answer depended on it.

"You're doing homework here," Dante said. He dropped his sneakers beside her and shook sand out of his hat. "On the last Friday of the summer."

"I'm doing homework anywhere. It's due tomorrow. If you must know, I have to figure out where this thing starts."

"Starts at the beach," he said, and walked toward the water.

She zoomed in until the pixels blurred. The line's left edge sat just above a gridline she couldn't read. Her first guess was three hundred fifty, and she wrote it down, then scratched it out, because guessing felt like prognosticating, like reading tea leaves, and the assignment was supposed to be about evidence. She needed the actual number. She texted Priya, who was already at orientation two states away, and got back a shrug emoji and "check the original station." That was Priya: never the answer, always the door the answer hid behind.

The original station took twenty minutes of searching on a phone with one bar of signal. She found it in an old report, a place on a volcano in Hawaii where someone had begun measuring the air in the late fifties. The first carbon dioxide reading at Mauna Loa, in March 1958, was about 313 parts per million. She said the number out loud to nobody, to the wind, and felt the graph snap into focus. The line that had looked abstract now had a birthdate. Three hundred thirteen, and now, when she followed the line right, the rise became arithmetic instead of atmosphere. She could finish. She could actually finish before dark.

Dante came back dripping and stood over her, casting a shadow across the screen. "Did you solve the world?"

"Three thirteen," she said. "That's where it starts. Now I subtract and that's how much it's gone up."

"That's it? That's the whole assignment?"

"There's a second part. I have to explain why the line goes up at all. Why the gas traps heat." She turned the phone toward him. "You want to hear it?"

He sat down on the wet sand beside the towel, not on the towel, which was its own small commentary. "Go ahead."

So she explained it, the way she'd been rehearsing it in her head all week: sunlight comes through, the earth warms, the warm surface sends heat back out, and the carbon dioxide in the air catches some of that outgoing heat and sends it back down, so the air holds on to more of it than it used to. She used her hands, the sun going down through them, the sand as the earth. Dante watched without expression.

"That's not what Dad's friends say," he said finally. "At the barbecue. They say the graph is fake and the scientists want grant money."

"You were at a barbecue listening to Dad's friends, and I'm at the beach doing the reading."

"I'm just telling you what they said."

"And I'm telling you the first reading was three hundred thirteen parts per million, and I can count." She said it harder than she meant to, and the wind took the sentence and thinned it to a diminuendo, until it was barely a sound between them.

He picked up a shell and turned it over. "So explain it to them. Sunday. They're coming over again."

That was the twist, and she saw it land in her own chest before she could disguise it. Her brother, who mocked the homework, was asking her to defend it in front of men twice her age who had already made up their minds. The deadline had just doubled: the paper at eight tomorrow, and Sunday afternoon at the grill with a paper plate in her hand.

"I can't explain anything to them," she said. "They'll say the volcano made the number up."

"Then say what you said to me. The sun through your hands. That was the first time I understood it."

She looked at the graph again, the sawtooth line rising off that small mark at three hundred thirteen. She did not know if she could change anyone's mind. She knew where the line started, and how to count what came after, and she knew that not knowing everything was not the same as knowing nothing. "Fine," she said. "Sunday. But you're standing next to me."

"Deal," Dante said, and threw the shell into the waves.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
The playground sat at the edge of the park where the riparian path ran along the river, and at ten in the morning it held one old man on a bench and one eighteen-year-old on the swings, neither of them swinging. Justin had the job listing on his phone. Crew member, Riverside Creamery, weekends and two evenings, interviews Thursday. He read it for the fourth time and put the phone face down on his thigh.

His grandfather had walked down with him because the doctor wanted him walking, and because Justin had asked. "Show me again," his grandfather said, and stood up from the bench with the careful motion of a man negotiating with his knees. Justin crossed the wood chips and put out his hand. His grandfather took it, frowned, and let go. "Like you're apologizing to my fingers."

"I'm working on it."

"You said that Tuesday."

Justin tried again. This time he gripped, and his grandfather held on a moment longer, testing. "Better. My father would have made you do it fifty times." He lowered himself back onto the bench. "There was a study. Two thousand. Psychologist named William Chaplin. Found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions." He said it the way he said the prices of things, a fact stored whole and offered without decoration. Then he took out his newspaper.

Justin sat down beside him. The Chaplin thing he could hold onto; it was checkable, it had edges. The rest of the interview was fog. Speak clearly. Answer the question they asked. Look them in the eye. His mother had said that last one three times at dinner until his sister remonstrated, saying that if she had to hear about Justin's eyes one more time she was eating in her room, and she had.

There was a girl at the far end of the playground, maybe six, doing loops on the spinning platform until she was too dizzy to stand. She staggered off it, laughed at nothing, and climbed back on. Justin watched her restart the loop and thought about how she never once checked whether anyone was watching.

A woman came by with a stroller and stopped at the bench to ask his grandfather about the river path, whether it went all the way to the footbridge, and Justin, without deciding to, said that it did, and that the riparian section past the oaks was shaded until about noon. He held her gaze while he said it. She thanked him and moved on, and his grandfather turned a page of the newspaper.

"You looked at her the whole time."

"Did I?"

"Whole time."

Justin hadn't noticed doing it, which seemed like the opposite of a problem, except that it meant he couldn't tell what had made the difference. Maybe it was that she'd wanted directions and he'd known the answer. There was no equivalent trick for "tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer" when he had never had a customer, difficult or otherwise. The application had asked for experience and he had written, honestly, none, and then felt the word sit on the page like a stain.

He got up and walked to the fence above the river. The summer was an interregnum, his history teacher had called it that in June, the stretch between one life and the next, and at the time it had sounded grand. Now it was nine weeks with nothing in them but this: get a job, save something, show up at college in the fall with a bank account that wasn't empty. The girl on the spinner went past behind him, shrieking, arms out.

When he turned around she had fallen off again and was lying flat in the wood chips, staring at the sky. He walked over, because she was small and alone, and she sat up before he reached her.

"Are you the boss of this park?" she asked.

"No."

"Do you want to be?"

"No," he said, and then, because it felt untrue, "Not of a park."

She nodded as if this settled something and went back to the spinner. His grandfather folded the newspaper. On the walk home, at the gate, Justin held out his hand, and his grandfather took it and did not let go until Justin had gripped it firm, and then he said, "Thursday," and Justin said, "Thursday," and they walked the rest of the way with the river running somewhere below them out of sight.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
Jade spread the two articles across the library table like cards she didn't trust herself to read. Both were about the same question, whether standardized testing narrowed what counted as learning, but they disagreed, and her assignment was to decide which argument held up better. The fluorescent light hummed above the periodicals, and somewhere behind her a printer churned out somebody else's deadline.

"That one first," Marcus said, dropping into the chair across from her. He ran the writing club's review sessions, and he'd appointed himself her editor for the afternoon. He tapped the article from the journal with the glossy cover. "You should lead with this. Its impact factor is way higher, so it's clearly the stronger source."

"Meaning what, exactly?" Jade asked. Marcus talked in numbers the way other people talked in weather, confidently, as though everyone already knew what the numbers meant.

He shrugged. "It's a ranking. Bigger number, better journal. Everybody uses it." He slid the second article, photocopied from a scruffy education journal, to the bottom of her stack. "Honestly, that one reads like a guy with a grudge and a tiny readership."

After he left to hassle a sophomore about thesis statements, Jade sat with the phrase turning over in her head. Higher number, better journal. She remembered being eleven, sitting on her grandmother's kitchen counter while her grandmother flipped through the mail, tossing half of it straight into the recycle bin. "Anything that says urgent in gold letters is begging," her grandmother had said, tearing a sweepstakes envelope in half without opening it. "The good news comes in plain envelopes." Jade had believed that for years, the way you believe things said over the smell of coffee and toast, and she was surprised to feel it resurface now, at a library table, over citations.

She pulled her laptop close and searched. What she found was simpler than Marcus had made it sound and stranger than she expected. The impact factor, she read, devised by Eugene Garfield, was the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years. She read the sentence three times. It was a measure of how often, on average, a journal's recent articles got cited in one year. That was all it was. It said nothing about whether the argument inside was careful, or whether the evidence had been gathered honestly, or whether the author had thought for six years or six weeks. A journal could have a big number for reasons that had nothing to do with the specific article in front of her, and a small journal could publish something that changed how she thought.

She turned back to the two articles themselves, and this time she read them differently, slower. The glossy one was smooth and confident, but its argument rested on a single large data set, and when Jade tried to imagine what the data left out, she found herself writing in the margin: problematize this. The scruffy one was clumsier, its author clearly impecunious in citations if not in purse, citing everyone who had ever touched the question. But buried in its ungainly middle section was a careful account of the historiography of testing, how the debate itself had been shaped over decades by who was allowed to publish and who wasn't, and that account made Jade stop chewing her pen. It problematized the very terms the glossy article took for granted.

The library emptied by degrees. Marcus came back for his backpack and paused at her table. "So you're leading with the big one, right?"

"Actually, no." She turned her draft toward him. "The impact factor is just the average number of citations in one year for articles from the previous two years. It measures traffic, not quality. This one has the weaker number but the stronger argument, I think. The other one assumes what it should prove."

Marcus looked at the draft, then at her, and she watched something shift behind his eyes, annoyance first, then something closer to interest. "Fine," he said. "Show me where the big one falls apart. If you can." He pulled out the chair again.

They worked until the announcement came that the library closed in fifteen minutes. Jade still hadn't decided how much weight to give the weaker article's one brilliant section against its many dull ones, and her draft ended on a paragraph she'd crossed out twice. She slid both articles into her bag, the glossy one no longer on top. At the door, Marcus held it open for her. "Same time Thursday," he said. "Bring the draft you're not sure about."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
story:
Parker found the cuff in the bathroom drawer on Tuesday, wedged between his father's old razors and a bottle of folic acid nobody had finished. His father had been home from the hospital for six days now, convalescing in the armchair by the window, his leg propped on an ottoman, a stack of unread magazines rising beside him like evidence of a life he expected to resume any moment. The doctor had sent the monitor home with instructions Parker's mother had relayed in fragments: twice a day, same arm, sit still. Nobody had said who would actually do it.

"I'll do it," Parker said that morning, kneeling on the rug while his father rolled up his sleeve. The cuff whirred and tightened, and his father grimaced the way he did when he didn't want to be fussed over, which was the way he did everything now. The screen settled on numbers. 142 over 88.

"That's stage 2," his father said, flat, as if reporting a score in a game neither of them followed.

Parker stared at the bottom number. Eighty-eight. Below ninety. He had absorbed, without ever being taught, that the second number was the one that mattered, the quiet one, the pressure when the heart was resting between beats. "The bottom one's fine, though," he said. "Isn't it?"

His father shrugged, which meant don't ask me, I'm the patient, not the mechanic. Parker carried the monitor to the kitchen and sat with his phone and a glass of orange juice he didn't really want. He looked up the numbers himself, thumbing past forums and ads, until he found the actual American guideline from 2017, the one the hospital pamphlet kept citing. He read it twice. Stage 2 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher. Either one. That small word did the whole work. His father's top number, 142, cleared the bar by two, and that was enough; the 88 sitting harmlessly beneath it changed nothing.

The strange part was how the sentence sat in his head afterward, less like a fact than like a rule of grammar he'd been misusing for years. He thought of his junior year, when he'd argued in a class debate that any policy with one good outcome deserved support, and Mr. Ruiz had written "and? or?" in the margin of his essay, a comment he'd never understood until now. Or. One condition met, the whole thing triggered. He wondered whether he'd been wrong then or whether the world simply ran on different logics in different rooms.

He went back in with a notebook and took the reading again that evening. 138 over 86. He wrote both down, then drew a small table, because his brain wanted columns. His father watched him from the chair, amused. "You're going to do this every day?"

"Twice a day," Parker said. "Doctor's orders, technically."

"Technically," his father repeated, and there was something in his voice that Parker recognized as the old resentment, thin now, worn down by the hospital and the stairs he still couldn't manage without pausing. Before the stroke, his father had eaten whatever he wanted, and Parker had eaten with him, two men under the happy hegemony of the drive-thru on Route 9, its neon sign a landmark of their Friday nights. His mother had never once said stop. Parker had thought, at the time, that her silence meant permission.

The readings were capricious at first, and he learned not to trust any single one. 139 over 84 in the morning, 146 over 90 after his father argued with the insurance company on the phone. Parker began noting what came before each number: the walk they'd taken to the mailbox, the low-sodium soup his mother had made, the afternoon his father snuck a bag of chips and the cuff reported it like an informer. Over two weeks the columns told a story he hadn't asked for. The readings eased down on the days they walked, crept up on the days they didn't, and the sodium seemed to matter in a slower way he couldn't yet read. He knew enough to say that something was moving. He couldn't say how much was the walking, how much the food, how much was just his father healing on his own schedule.

On a Thursday, nineteen days in, the morning reading was 131 over 82. His father looked at it for a long time, his thumb moving over the screen as if he could smear the number into something better or worse. Parker waited, notebook open, the pen warm in his hand.

"Still not normal," his father said.

"Still not stage 2," Parker said, and turned the notebook toward the window so his father could see the whole column falling, day by day, like a staircase he was climbing down.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
The trail climbed through fog that thinned and thickened again with the wind, so that the ocean appeared and vanished like something deciding whether to be seen. Laurence had chosen it because it was steep enough to hurt, and because Dev had said, when she texted him last night, that if she was going to freeze again she might as well freeze somewhere beautiful. That was Dev's way of being kind, which was to make the kindness into a joke and then walk faster so you couldn't examine it.

"Round two," he said, three switchbacks up. He took the folded paper out of his jacket, the one she'd printed at the library, and shook it open against his knee. "I'm the skeptic. You're you. Go."

"I'm not ready on a slope."

"The tournament's Saturday. Slopes are all we have." He cleared his throat and put on the voice, the reasonable one, the one that had dismantled her last week in the empty classroom while Mr. Okafor watched and said nothing. "My opponent claims carbon dioxide is driving warming. But the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere isn't carbon dioxide at all. It's water vapor. So isn't the real cause of warming just water?"

Her mouth went dry the way it had in the classroom, and she hated that her body kept its own records. She stopped walking and looked out at the water, where a line of dark birds rode the swells offshore, pelagic things that never came to land except to breed, and she thought about how much of the world ran on systems you couldn't see from where you stood.

"No," she said. "Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it's not the one starting it. It acts mainly as a feedback. Warmer air holds more water vapor, and that amplifies warming that other gases, like carbon dioxide, started." She heard the sentence land and held still, waiting to find out whether it had come out whole.

Dev lowered the paper. "Again, but slower. Like you're talking to a judge who got a B minus in chemistry."

She said it again, slower, and then a third time with her hands open, the way she'd watched the senior captain do it: carbon dioxide starts the warming, the air warms, warmer air holds more water vapor, and the added vapor amplifies what was started. "The skeptic makes it sound like abundance equals cause," she said. "But the water vapor is answering, not asking."

"Huh," Dev said, which from him was applause. He handed her the paper. "Now the graph."

The printout showed carbon dioxide across the last century, a curve climbing in small patient steps, with a fine sawtooth jitter running along it like a pulse. Last week she had called it "a rise," and the skeptic had pounced on her vagueness, asking her what the axis meant, and she had stood there silent while the clock ran. She traced the line now with one finger, naming the parts out loud: the vertical axis was concentration, the horizontal was time, the little annual wobble was the land breathing, the overall trend the thing that mattered. She titrated her words as she went, a small precise amount at a time, because she'd learned that dumping the whole explanation at once drowned people, and a judge who felt drowned reached for whatever floated nearest, which was usually the other side.

"You're doing the thing," Dev said.

"What thing."

"The thing where you get good at something and immediately start wondering if you were lazy before." He sat down on a root and unwrapped a granola bar. She stayed standing, breathing hard, because the climb was still in her legs and because what he'd said was true in a way she hadn't decided how to hold. She had skipped the study session in September to drive to the coast with Priya, and on the drive home Priya had said the article she was reading was basically historiography, a story scientists told about their own past mistakes, and Laurence had said that sounded like an excuse not to learn the science, and Priya had said maybe the excuse and the science could both be true. They hadn't argued. They had just gone quiet with the radio on. She still didn't know which of them had been right, and she noticed she didn't much want the answer settled, the way she did want the graph settled, its line rising without apology.

"One more round," she said. "Water vapor again. Give me the harder version."

Dev stood, brushed off his knees, and became the skeptic so completely that his shoulders changed. "If water vapor amplifies the warming," he said, "isn't your side admitting the water does the heavy lifting?"

She opened her mouth, and the fog came in off the water and swallowed the birds, and she began to answer.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Alexandre spread the coins across the kitchen table after dinner, sliding his mother's sugar bowl to one side to make room. He had borrowed a book from the library about directing, and the book had said something he could not stop turning over: that blocking, the word itself, came from nineteenth-century directors like W. S. Gilbert, who planned whole scenes on a model stage, using a small block to stand for each actor. Gilbert had moved the blocks before he ever moved a person. Alexandre set down a two-euro coin for Judith, a one-euro coin for Tomas, and a bottle cap for the door everyone kept forgetting was there.

The trouble had begun on Tuesday, in the church hall where the drama group rehearsed. Alexandre had been handed the one-act because Ms. Ferrand said someone younger should try directing, and he had said yes before he understood what yes would cost him. Judith, who was seventeen and had been in six plays, did not want to be told where to stand. Tomas wanted to be told everything. And the script, a slight thing about two siblings dividing their dead father's toolbox, kept going flat whenever the two of them stood where Alexandre had put them, which was almost everywhere he put them.

"You're moving us like furniture," Judith had said, arms crossed, the third time he'd asked her to cross downstage left. She was not irascible by nature, but three rehearsals of being arranged had brought it out in her, a shortness that arrived before her words did.

He had gone home and read instead of arguing, and that was where Gilbert was waiting, patient in a paperback with a cracked spine. Alexandre turned the bottle cap, walked the two-euro coin toward it, and watched the imagined scene from above, the way a director at a model stage would see it: not faces, only distances. The whole third page of the script, he realized, was a scene about not touching, and he had been blocking it as if the characters wanted to be close. The artifice of the staging, the neat crosses he'd designed because they looked composed from the tenth row, had been fighting the play. He had been arranging a picture. The scene wanted an argument held still.

On Thursday he came to the hall with the coins in his jacket pocket and a card table under his arm. He set the table up in front of the two actors, poured the coins out, and laid out the third page the way he'd rehearsed it at his kitchen table. "This is you," he said, tapping the two-euro coin. "And this is Tomas. Watch."

"You brought monopoly money to rehearsal," Judith said, but she leaned in.

"I read that the word blocking comes from Gilbert," Alexandre said. "Nineteenth-century. He used a model stage and a block for each actor." He moved the coin three steps away from the smaller one and left it there. "So page three. They don't cross to each other. Nobody crosses the whole page. They want the toolbox and they want the other one to hand it over, and neither one moves first."

Tomas, who had been quiet all week, sat down at the card table and nudged the bottle cap with one finger. "Then the door should be on this side," he said. "If she won't go to him, the door has to be behind her, so leaving is easy and she still doesn't do it."

"Try it," Alexandre said, and Judith, who had opened her mouth to object, closed it, picked up the two-euro coin, and moved it herself, half a step, angling it so it faced neither the smaller coin nor the door. She looked at the little triangle of metal for a long moment.

"Like that," she said. "Not facing him. That's crueler."

They ran the page standing, no table between them, only the shape the coins had made. Judith delivered the line about the hammer with her back half-turned, and the hall, which had been stubborn and dead all week, went quiet in a way Alexandre could feel in his sternum. Afterward Judith did not compliment him, which he understood was its own kind of verdict. She picked up the two-euro coin from the table and pressed it into his palm.

"Bring these every rehearsal," she said.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Raising interest rates tends to strengthen a country's currency by attracting foreign savings, which makes imports cheaper and puts downward pressure on prices.
story:
The kitchen at her grandfather's house smelled of coffee and newsprint, the way it had every summer since Savannah could remember. She spread the Lisbon brochures across the table, next to his crossword, and opened the currency app on her phone for the fourth time that morning. The dollar was buying more euros than it had in the spring, enough more that her spreadsheet for the school trip had gone from impossible to merely terrifying. She had a job at the garden center, sixty dollars a week, and she had done the arithmetic so many times the numbers felt like a bruise.

"Still counting other people's money," her grandfather said, not looking up from the crossword. His smile was sardonic, the kind he wore when he wanted to be teased out of it. He had retired from the bank in town before Savannah was born, and he treated every question about money as an invitation to dodge.

She turned the phone toward him. "Look. In March the trip was going to cost me two hundred more than it does now. The euro got cheaper for us. Why?"

He filled in a word, tapped the pen twice against the table, and said nothing. That was his way of saying figure it out yourself.

Savannah slid the brochures into her bag and walked to the window. On the radio, half heard, a man had said something that morning about the central bank and interest rates, and she had let it wash past her the way school announcements washed past her, and now it snagged on something. She took out a notebook and wrote it down in her looping, fast handwriting, because that was how she thought, with the pen moving. The bank had raised rates. Then, over the following weeks, the exchange rate had shifted in her favor. She sat very still with her pen hovering, and the kitchen went quiet enough that she could hear the refrigerator hum.

"Grandpa," she said slowly, "when rates go up, who wants to move their money here?"

He set down the crossword. "People with savings," he said, and went back to seven across.

She wrote it out like a proof, the way Ms. Okonjo made them do in geometry. Higher rates, foreign savings comes in to earn them. All that money coming in makes the dollar stronger. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper. Cheaper imports push prices down, which is the whole point, because prices have been climbing all year, her mother's grocery bills, the gas for the car, the trip itself. She read the chain back to herself and felt the small, clean click of it holding together. Then she called Priya, because explaining a thing to someone was the only way to be sure she understood it.

"So the bank raises rates, right," she said into the phone, pacing between the table and the window, "and that pulls foreign savings in, because everyone wants to earn the higher interest here. All that money coming in strengthens our currency. A stronger currency makes imports cheaper, and cheaper imports put downward pressure on prices. That's how it fights inflation. That's why the euro got cheaper for us." Priya asked a question about whether it hurt anyone, and Savannah paused, because she had been about to say no.

Her grandfather had a mortgage he complained about, and Priya's brother was trying to get a loan for a food truck, and her own mother had said in April, flatly, that rate hikes were for people who already had money. She turned and asked him, point blank, whether raising rates was a good thing. He shrugged and said it was a bad thing for him and his mortgage, and she pushed back, and they argued mildly over the cold coffee, and then he did something he almost never did. He changed his mind, partway, out loud. "It costs me," he said, "and it costs your mother's grocery bill nothing, in the end, if it works. Maybe both things are true." Savannah said she thought both things were true too, and that she could not prove which one weighed more, and that this bothered her more than any equation ever had.

Later, while he was out at his flu shot appointment, complaining on the phone beforehand that they were injecting him with a dead antigen to trick his body, Savannah cleaned the table and found an envelope that had slid under the fruit bowl. It was thick, and it was addressed to her in his handwriting, and she held it for a long moment without opening it, the way you hold something you suspect will change your arithmetic. Inside was cash, hundreds in twenties, and a note in pencil: Your grandmother started this the year she got sick. She wanted you to see the azulejos. She thought a trip like that could emancipate a person from thinking their whole life was going to be the town they grew up in.

She counted it twice. It was almost exactly the gap in her spreadsheet, the one she had been telling no one about, the one she had been planning to solve by selling her camera. When he came back through the door, rubbing his shoulder and grumbling about nurses, she was standing at the window with the app open again, and she watched the exchange rate flicker and settle, and she said, "I found the envelope."

He hung up his coat. "I know," he said. "I watched you not open it for ten minutes through the window. You counted it like a bank teller."

"I'm taking it," Savannah said, and folded the envelope into her back pocket, and put the brochures back on the table, one by one, square with the edges, like she was dealing cards.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
The lasagna had gone cold at Gabriella's end of the table, which her mother noticed before anyone else did. "You're not eating," her mother said, not querulous, just observing, the way she observed everything at these Thursday dinners, as though the family were a small weather system she was tracking.

"I ate at practice," Gabriella said, which was technically true, in the sense that she had swallowed half a granola bar while watching Priya run the routine again.

"So tell us about regionals," her father said, reaching for the bread. "Two weeks?"

"Two weeks." Gabriella turned her fork over on the plate. "We're doing the doubles pass. Priya and me. Except Priya isn't speaking to me, so that's going well."

Her brother Daniel looked up from his phone, and she knew that look, the look of someone who had been waiting all evening for a conversational opening. He was home from his first semester of college and had become insufferable about it, forwarding everyone articles as though he were the first person to discover reading. "What did you say to her?" he asked.

"Nothing. I mean, I said her landings were beautiful, and her timing was great, and her arms were, I don't know, elegant, and then I said her round-off was crooked and she keeps drifting left." Gabriella shrugged. "One thing. I said one thing out of five."

Daniel set the phone down, screen up, and she saw a page of text on it, some article with a graph. "I just read this review for my psych class," he said. "A 2001 review, it was led by Roy Baumeister, and it was called 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good.' It found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size."

"So?"

"So you gave her five compliments and one criticism, and she remembered the criticism. That's the whole thing. Bad is stronger than good."

"That's depressing," their mother said, refilling the water glasses.

"It's not depressing, it's just how it works." Daniel turned the phone toward Gabriella. "Look, one bad thing isn't balanced by one good thing of the same size. You'd need more. I'm not saying it's fair."

Gabriella looked at the graph without really reading it. She had been litigating the argument in her head all afternoon, building the case that she had done nothing wrong, that honest feedback was part of being a teammate, that Priya was being thin-skinned. But the case kept collapsing, because underneath it was a postulate she hadn't examined: that if she stacked up enough nice words, the hard word would weigh less. Priya hadn't heard any of the nice words. Priya had heard crooked, and drifting, and left.

She pushed her plate away. "Can I be excused?"

"You can eat your lasagna first," her mother said, so Gabriella ate the lasagna, mechanically, while Daniel described his dorm and his roommate's habit of microwaving fish, and then she carried her plate to the sink and went out to the back steps with her phone.

The evening air smelled like the neighbor's cut grass. She sat on the top step and did not call Priya right away, because she wanted to get the words in order. Her first instinct was to apologize for the round-off comment, but that felt wrong too, because the round-off was crooked, and they had regionals in two weeks, and lying to a teammate was its own kind of unkindness. What she wanted, she realized, was a way to be honest that didn't land like a slap. Not softer truths. Same truth, better delivery.

She called.

Priya answered on the fourth ring, which meant she had watched the phone and decided. "What."

"I'm sorry about today," Gabriella said. "Not for what I said. For how I said it. I dumped everything at once and the criticism was the last thing, so it's the thing you heard, and I get that now. My brother says there's actual research on it." She paused. "But here's the thing, and tell me if this is okay. Your round-off drifts left. Maybe six inches. Every time. It's the only thing between you and that pass being clean."

There was a long silence, long enough that Gabriella could hear a television going somewhere in Priya's house.

"You counted?" Priya said finally.

"What?"

"You watched enough to know it's every time, and how far. You actually watched."

"Well, yeah. You're my partner."

Another silence, and then Priya said, "I was going to text you tonight and ask you to help me fix it. I've known for two weeks. I just didn't want to be the one to say it out loud."

Gabriella started laughing, there on the steps, the screen door glowing yellow behind her. "So you stopped talking to me for six hours because I said the thing you were already thinking."

"That's completely different," Priya said. "Practice at eight tomorrow. Bring the crooked round-off."

"It's your round-off."

"Not anymore," Priya said, and hung up.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
The library at three o'clock was spartan in a way John liked: bare tables, gray carpet, the hum of the radiators doing all the talking. He spread his draft across a carrel near the window, six pages of an argument about whether Carnegie should be lionized as a philanthropist or remembered as the man whose guards fired on striking workers at Homestead. Mr. Reyes had insisted the paper take a position, real footnotes, a bibliography in Chicago style. John had never done any of it.

He had done the reading, at least. Two biographies that treated Carnegie like a saint, and one slim book by a labor historian that worked as a counterpoint, arguing the libraries he built were paid for twice, once by steel profits and once by the men who made them. John's thesis was that both versions were true and that the second one had been buried on purpose. He thought that was a position. He hoped Mr. Reyes would think so too.

The problem was the notes. He had opened the footnote tool in his word processor, dropped a superscript number into a sentence, and typed his citation. But when he scrolled on, the note was not at the bottom of the page where the number was. Every note he added had slid to the end of the document, piling up on the last page in a block. He pressed print to see it on paper, and there it was: page two, the little raised 4, and then nothing beneath it until page eight.

Priya from his history class was two tables over with a highlighter and a bag of pretzels. He carried the pages over. "Is this allowed? My citations aren't where I put them."

She looked. "Mine did that too. I panicked, then I didn't fix it."

"You didn't fix it?"

"Look at the style sheet Reyes gave us." She dug through her binder and flattened a photocopied page. "A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs. An endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter." She tapped it. "So what you've got, all bunched at the end, is endnotes. They're a real thing. Just not the thing he asked for."

"So I have to make them be footnotes."

"Or ask if endnotes are okay."

He stood there holding his own pages, the wind outside pushing at the window, a groundskeeper raking leaves against the fence. He didn't want to ask. Asking felt like admitting he didn't know the difference, and now he did know the difference, which was somehow worse.

He went back to the carrel and hunted through the menus. There was a dropdown he had scrolled past three times, a setting for where notes went, and he changed it and reprinted. The numbers stayed in his sentences and the citations dropped to the bottoms of their own pages, each one anchored where it belonged. He read the page differently now. When he claimed the Homestead guards were Pinkertons, the source sat right there under his thumb, a few centimeters away, instead of hiding six pages back. The argument felt heavier. Harder to wave off.

But the last of his notes, the long one where he admitted the record on Carnegie's personal role at Homestead was contested, that some historians put the decision in Frick's hands alone, he left at the end. He reformatted it as an endnote deliberately, and in the text after it he wrote that the uncertainty belonged at some distance from his claim, because he was not sure, and he did not want the small print of a footnote to make it look like he was. He would find out on Monday whether that counted as a position or a dodge.

Priya passed his table on her way out. "Fixed?"

"Some of it," he said, and squared the pages against the edge of the carrel.

The librarian began clicking off the banks of lights from the far wall, one section going dark, then the next, and John kept his lamp on and kept reading.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
Olivia spread the ten paintings across her grandmother's dining room table, weighting the corners with teacups so the paper would not curl. The theme was supposed to be doors, which had seemed brilliant in July when she'd started, and now, in the last week of August, seemed like something she had invented to avoid thinking about anything at all. The application required ten works around a single idea plus a statement, and the deadline was Friday.

Her grandmother came in with a tray of lemonade, set it down among the paintings without looking at any of them for long. "Which one is the best," she said, not as a question but as an instruction, the way she asked everything.

"The blue one," Olivia said. "The screen door with the light behind it." She had painted it the morning after the funeral, before anyone else was awake, standing at the kitchen sink where her grandfather used to stand. She had not told anyone that, including herself.

The application form had two separate boxes. One said wall card, fifty to one hundred words. The other said full statement, five hundred to one thousand words. Olivia had written one paragraph of about three hundred words, and pasted it into both boxes, and a friend from her class had messaged her back within an hour: they won't take it like that, the wall card cuts you off. Olivia had stared at the message in her grandmother's hallway, where the wallpaper smelled faintly of lavender and dust, and understood that she had been treating the statement as a chore rather than as part of the work.

"It's like a résumé," her grandmother said at dinner, sawing at a pork chop. "You don't give the whole story to someone who stops you at the post office." This was the extent of her sagacity on the subject, and it was enough.
