Olivia went to bed thinking about the difference between someone who stops you at the post office and someone who sits down with your file, and she got up early and wrote two statements instead of one.

The short one she could do. Sixty words about doors as thresholds, about standing on either side of a decision. She read it aloud in the empty kitchen and it sounded like someone else, someone brisk and certain. The long one defeated her. Every time she reached five hundred words she found she had only restated the first paragraph in a more profligate vocabulary, adjectives stacked on adjectives, as if quantity could stand in for actually knowing what she meant.

On Thursday she went looking for the iron in the hall closet and found instead a shoebox of her grandmother's things, and beneath the doilies and the dead fountain pens, a folder of photographs. They were paintings. Her grandmother's paintings, from before Olivia was born: a whole series of windows, watercolor, dated on the backs in her grandfather's handwriting. Twenty of them. Maybe thirty. Olivia sat down on the hall floor with the box in her lap and did not call anyone.

"You went through my closet," her grandmother said that evening, from the doorway of the kitchen. It was not an accusation. She came in and sat across from Olivia and turned the photographs around so they faced her, one at a time, like dealing cards.

"Why did you stop?"

Her grandmother looked at the window in the photograph, a kitchen window with geraniums, the same geraniums that were, as far as Olivia knew, still in the actual kitchen window. "He asked me to," she said. "Not in so many words. There was the shop, and then your mother, and a person verbalizes a thing once or twice and then it's decided for her." She squared the photographs against the table edge. "Write your statement. I'll read it."

Olivia did not sleep much that night. She sat at the dining room table with the screen door painting in front of her and wrote the long statement from the beginning, and this time it was not about thresholds at all. It was about doors as the things you close, the choices that hold their shape after you've walked away from them, and she wrote six hundred words in forty minutes and hated some of it and kept it anyway because it was true. Then she cut the short one down to the bone, and it no longer matched the long one exactly, and she decided that was fine, that maybe that was even the point.

In the morning her grandmother read both versions at the table while Olivia pretended to wash dishes that were already clean. "The short one lies a little," her grandmother said finally. "The long one doesn't." She set the pages side by side. "Which one is you?"

Olivia looked at them. The short one said the work was about transition and possibility. The long one said the work was about her grandfather's screen door and her grandmother's windows and the way her family had always mistaken closing things for keeping them safe. Both were hers. She could not say which one was more hers, and she did not think she was supposed to be able to.

"I don't know yet," she said.

Her grandmother nodded slowly, the way she nodded at weather she had seen coming. Then she picked up one of the photographs, the kitchen window with the geraniums, and set it in front of the screen door painting so the two images leaned against the teacups, window beside door, and pushed both of them an inch toward Olivia across the table.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
story:
The worksheet had thirty-eight slots for ATP, and Maxime kept getting thirty-six. He counted again at the table beside the giant mitochondria model, a cutaway the size of a small car, its inner membrane folded into ridges you could have climbed like a jungle gym. He was here because his biology teacher offered extra credit for the museum's cellular respiration trail, and because his mother had said a boy about to start college should learn to do things alone, and because both of those reasons felt smaller than the truth, which was that he had nearly failed the unit test and wanted, quietly, to prove something to no one in particular.

His phone buzzed against the table. A message from his sister Amelie, who was spending her gap year in Lisbon and sent long texts the way other people sent postcards: "I met a woman at the hostel who repairs church organs. She says the pipes are like a body, each one a different length, and I keep thinking about Dad teaching us piano and how I quit and you didn't. Do you ever regret sticking with it? I regret quitting and I also don't. Both are true at once and it's very annoying." He read it twice, then set the phone face down and picked up his pencil.

The trail began at glycolysis. A placard showed one glucose molecule, six carbons, splitting into two three-carbon sugars, and then the sugars becoming something called pyruvate. He copied the arrows carefully, the way he copied everything, and his tally sheet gained a modest two ATP. Fine. Then came a step he had skated over in class: pyruvate became acetyl-CoA. He wrote it down. Below it, the citric acid cycle, drawn as a wheel with eight spokes, each spoke a reaction, each turn releasing a little carbon dioxide and banking a little energy.

He worked the wheel once, counting. One ATP per turn, plus the electron carriers that would later feed the big payoff. He added the numbers at the final station, the folded membrane where the carriers surrendered their electrons. Thirty-eight, again. Thirty-six was nowhere on the placard; thirty-eight was what his own arithmetic kept insisting. He checked his carrier counts twice. The problem, he suspected, was somewhere upstream, in the part he had copied without thinking.

A girl about his age appeared at the wheel with her own worksheet, chewing her pencil. She was wearing a museum volunteer shirt two sizes too large, which gave her a boxy, borrowed morphology, like a kid dressed by an older sibling. She frowned at the placard, then at him. "Is your total coming out wrong too?" she asked. "Mine's off by exactly the amount of one turn of this thing."

"Mine's off by more than that," Maxime said, and then stopped. Off by one turn. He looked at his glycolysis notes, at the glucose splitting in two, at the pyruvate, at the acetyl-CoA. One glucose made not one acetyl-CoA but two, and each one entered the cycle separately, so the wheel had to be counted twice. He flipped his pencil over and erased. "The cycle turns twice for every glucose," he said, almost to himself. "Everything after the split happens two times."

The volunteer, whose name tag said Dara, leaned over his sheet. "That's it. That's my whole error, I only went around once." She laughed, a short startled sound, and copied his correction onto her page with the concentration of someone reversing a conviction. She told him she was volunteering because she wanted to study medicine and her grades were good but her applications needed "something with texture," a word she used without embarrassment, and he found he liked that about her. They walked the rest of the trail together, past a station about enzymes, where a display claimed that a single enzyme could catalyze thousands of reactions per second, and Dara said that made her feel both very small and very busy.

At the end they sat on a bench beneath a banner that read ENERGY WITHIN, which Maxime thought was a little grandiose for a room about sugar, though he admitted to himself that the wheel turning twice, the doubling of everything after the split, did have a strange symmetry to it, a kind of hidden arithmetic inside the body. He texted Amelie back: "I don't regret the piano. Or I regret it sometimes and mostly I don't. Also I learned today that one sugar becomes two and everything downstream counts double, which is not a metaphor, but you can have it if you want one."

She replied with a photo of the organ pipes and one line: "Send me the worksheet when you're done, I want to see the wheel." Dara was rechecking her totals at the table, lips moving, pencil hovering. Maxime watched her count the wheel twice, then a third time, as if to be sure the doubling would hold.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
The art room smelled of turpentine and the cold radiators of a building that had given up on October. Ella spread her nine paintings across two tables, all of them the copper beech outside the library window, and stood back with the list Ms. Okafor had taped to the wall: ten works, one theme, an artist's statement, due Friday. It was Tuesday. She had nine paintings and no statement, and the theme she had written in her sketchbook, "the tree at different times," looked flimsy now that it was spelled out in ink.

"It's the same tree nine times," said Priya, sliding her own portfolio box under the table with her knee. "I mean, I like them. But is it enough variety?"

Ella turned the paintings so they ran in order, dawn to dusk. In the first the beech was a bruise of violet; by the fifth the leaves had gone the flat gold of late afternoon; in the last it stood against a sky the color of dishwater, its trunk gone blue. Same tree, same angle, same bench with its missing slat. She had thought the sameness was the point, the way a person you see every day looks different and doesn't.

"That's literally what he did," said Marcus from the window, where he was cutting mats with a sardonic efficiency, as though the deadline were a personal nemesis he intended to defeat by four o'clock. "Monet. He painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral, in 1892 and 1893. Same facade, different light, different times of day and year."

"More than thirty," Ella said.

"Look it up, I don't care. We did him in art history last spring." He scored the matboard and snapped it clean. "Everyone in that class painted a haystack afterward. It was grim."

Ella sat down at one of the scarred tables and opened her laptop, but she didn't type right away. She watched Marcus instead, who had moved on to prying open a tin of pins with a ruler, and she thought about how a fact could be a door or could just be a fact, depending on whether you were willing to walk through it. She typed the cathedral into the search bar. The images loaded in a grid, thirty-some facades, stone that was pink, then butter-yellow, then a ghostly white, and she understood suddenly that the building had almost nothing to do with it. Monet had painted the light and let the cathedral reify it, give it edges, make a shape you could hang on a wall.

Priya leaned over her shoulder. "Okay, so your tree is your cathedral."

"Sort of." Ella scrolled slowly. "But he went back to the same spot over two years. Seasons, not just hours. Mine are all from the last three weeks. It's all September." She heard the doubt in her own voice and let it sit there instead of papering over it.

"So paint two more and lie about when you did them," Marcus said, not looking up.

"I can't lie in an artist's statement. It's the one place you can't lie."

"Then paint fast."

Ella looked out the window at the beech, at the low sun turning the leaves the exact amber of painting number five, and she did the math. Two paintings in three days. One she could do tomorrow at dawn, before first period, which would give her a cold-blue version to bookend the gold ones. The other she couldn't fake: what she wanted was the tree in November, bare, and November was five weeks away. She sat with that for a moment, the gap between what the theme wanted and what the deadline allowed, and she found she wasn't panicked by it. She was interested in it. That felt like information.

She pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward her and wrote, "These paintings look at one tree, but the tree is not quite the subject," and stopped, because the next sentence was where she'd have to decide what was. Light, probably. Or attention. Or the fact that she had walked past that tree every school day for four years and only started seeing it when she made herself stand still and look.

Priya was gathering her things, shrugging on a coat with a broken zipper. "Dawn tomorrow? I'll let you in the side door. Mr. Hale leaves it unlocked for the swim team."

"Six forty," Ella said. "Bring the bad coffee from the machine, not the worse coffee."

Priya held up two fingers in a victory sign and pushed out into the hallway, and Ella turned back to the half-written sentence, picked up her pencil, and crossed out everything after "subject."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
The math club met on Tuesdays in the library annex, a room that smelled of old laminate and radiator dust, and Maika arrived early because Priya had asked her to check a problem set before the session started. Priya slid the pages across the table with the particular confidence of someone who believed she had finished something, and Maika read the first line and felt her stomach drop in a way that was not unpleasant.

"Question four," Maika said. "You wrote that the derivative of x cubed is x squared."

"That's what it is, isn't it? You just, like, drop the exponent down in front."

Maika turned the page toward the window light. Every problem on the sheet had the same shape of error, neat and consistent, which was almost worse than being wrong randomly. She remembered her own sheet two weeks ago, the night her father had come home late from the hospital and she had sat at the kitchen table until midnight wanting the work to be right because so much else wasn't. She had made a mistake then too, though a different one, and had ascribed her stubbornness that night to diligence when it was really something closer to pride.

"Here," she said, pulling a clean sheet toward her. "Watch." She wrote x cubed, then an arrow, then 3x squared. "The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1. So the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared. You kept the power the same. You have to lower it by one."

Priya frowned at the paper. "Lower it by one."

"Every single problem. Six problems, same thing."

Behind them, two juniors were arguing about whether a certain curve ever touched its asymptote, their voices rising the way voices did in the annex, which was impervious to shushing because Ms. Okafor had long ago decided the argument was the point. Maika half listened. The asymptote question was one of those things she liked precisely because the answer was no and also kind of yes, depending on what you meant by touch, and she was still deciding whether she found that satisfying or irritating.

Priya was redoing the first problem, tongue between her teeth. "Okay. So then for the maximum thing, I set it equal to zero and solve?"

"You set the derivative equal to zero. That's where the curve levels out." Maika drew the curve freehand, a hill rising and falling, and marked the flat place at the top. "Here. The slope is zero right there, so that's your maximum."

"That's it? That seems too easy."

"It is easy," Maika said. "That's the part that made me suspicious."

She had spent the first month of calculus distrusting the power rule the way she distrusted people who were charming immediately. It felt like getting something for nothing, a whole exponent tamed in one motion. Her old way of thinking about math had been slow and scrupulous, plotting points, watching the pattern emerge from the wreckage of arithmetic, and the new way was a shortcut that arrived without showing its work. What she had slowly concluded, sitting where Priya sat now, was that both ways were true at once: the rule was a kind of trust extended in advance, and the checking was how you earned it back.

Priya worked the algebra. The club's president, Daniel, drifted over and stood behind them with his arms crossed, radiating the authority of a senior who had taken AP Calculus as a sophomore. "She's got it," he said, before Priya had finished writing.

"Let her finish," Maika said, and was a little surprised at how sharp it came out. Daniel raised his eyebrows and retreated to the whiteboard, where he began sketching the asymptote argument for the juniors, drawing the curve closer and closer to its line without ever letting them meet.

"Seven fifty," Priya read off her calculator. "The maximum is at x equals seven fifty?"

"Check it against the original function." Maika watched her substitute, square the decimal, multiply. Last year, in the spring, she had helped her younger brother with algebra every evening, and one night he had said, without looking up, that she explained things better than their mother did, and she had not known whether to be pleased. She thought about that now, the small theft of it, the compliment that ascribed to her a patience she wasn't sure she'd actually earned. She had been tired that whole spring. Some evenings she had only pretended to check his work.

"It checks," Priya said. "Oh. Oh, that's satisfying." She looked up at Maika with the particular brightness of someone who has just watched a machine work for the first time. "So every one of my problems was wrong in the same way."

"Every one. But the algebra underneath was clean. Fix the power and it all goes through."

"Could have been worse, then." Priya pulled the sheet back and began correcting in green ink, unhurried, as though the error had been a stylistic choice she was now revising. At the whiteboard Daniel was saying, "It gets infinitely close," and one of the juniors was saying, "But it never gets there," and Maika listened to them go around it, neither of them wrong, neither of them done.

The radiator ticked. Priya crossed out her last x squared, wrote 3x squared above it, and underlined the maximum twice.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: According to Acts 15 in the New Testament, a meeting of the early church in Jerusalem decided that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised.
story:
The community hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Gavin had claimed the corner table by the folding doors because it was the only one where the fluorescent light didn't buzz directly overhead. In front of him lay a photocopied page of Acts 15, highlighted in three colors, though the colors no longer meant anything. Saturday debate practice had thinned to four people: Mr. Okonkwo's niece Priya, a homeschooled kid named Daniel, and Ruth, who was here only because her mother ran the hall's rental calendar and had refused to drive twice.

Gavin's problem was specific. At the interchurch tournament in three weeks, he had to argue that the rules of an ancient religious text could still bind modern life, and Daniel, drawing for the opposing side, had already beaten him twice in scrimmage. Daniel's argument was simple and Gavin hadn't found a crack in it. Circumcision, Daniel said, was commanded in Genesis, plain as a sentence could be, and if you claimed the old rules still applied, you had to take that one too, or admit you were picking and choosing according to taste. Every time Gavin tried to answer, he ended up sounding like a man describing a house he was simultaneously dismantling.

Priya read the page upside down from across the table. "What's the highlighter even for," she said. "It looks like a crime scene."

"For confidence," Gavin said, and turned the paper face down.

He had grown up with the verse everyone quoted, the one about the law being a schoolmaster, and he had heard his pastor use it to wave away questions about shellfish and mixed fabrics. But the pastor's version was fog. It asserted a conclusion and called the fog mystery. What Gavin wanted, and had wanted since he was maybe twelve, was a reason that lived inside the text itself, one that didn't require him to step outside and appeal to what felt right, because feelings were exactly what Daniel accused him of following.

The week before, hunting through the New Testament for ammunition, he had found Acts 15 almost by accident. A dispute had broken out in Antioch, he read, certain believers insisting that non-Jewish converts had to be circumcised, and the matter was carried to a meeting in Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders gathered to consider it. Gavin read the chapter twice on the bus home. The meeting decided that non-Jewish converts did not need to be circumcised. He sat with that for a long moment, because it changed something. The believers themselves had debated which old rules still applied, and they had done the deciding inside the story, not outside it. Daniel's tidy picture of a text that either ruled everything or ruled nothing was, apparently, a picture the text itself declined to sit for.

At the next practice he laid the page flat between their coffee cups. "Acts fifteen," he said. "A meeting of the early church in Jerusalem decided that non-Jewish converts to Christianity did not need to be circumcised."

Daniel read it twice, and Gavin watched him read it, the way his eyes went back to the top and started over. "That's," Daniel began, and stopped. "That's them changing the rule."

"That's them deciding which rule carried," Gavin said. "Which is what you're saying can't be done."

"It's what you're saying they did." Daniel frowned at the page as though it had misled him personally. But he didn't dismiss it, and that was the strange part. He argued the next twenty minutes with real engagement instead of reflex, and when Priya said his objections were becoming intransigent, he actually laughed and conceded the point. What he would not concede was the danger in Gavin's discovery. If a rule could be weighed and found conditional once, Daniel said, then every rule afterward lived under that shadow, and the exceptions could metastasize until nothing was left that anyone had to obey. Gavin admitted the shadow was real. He hadn't come away with certainty; he'd come away with a tradition that argued with itself in its own pages, which was either its weakness or its whole character, and he genuinely did not know which.

Ruth, who had been listening from the stage steps while pretending to do inventory, came over before they packed up. "So did you win?" she asked.

"Not exactly," Gavin said. "I think I found out the argument doesn't end. The Jerusalem meeting didn't end it either. They decided one thing and kept arguing about everything after."

"That sounds exhausting," Ruth said.

Daniel zipped his bag. "It sounds like a forfeit," he said, but he said it quietly, and he folded his copy of the page in quarters and put it in his pocket instead of the recycling bin. At the door he turned around. "Same time next week. Bring the rest of the chapter."

Gavin began stacking the chairs.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
The kitchen clock said 6:40, and Emma's chem quiz was first period tomorrow, which gave her roughly fifteen hours to understand something she had been pretending to understand for two weeks. She spread her notebook across her grandmother's oilcloth-covered table, between a bowl of green tomatoes and a jar of buttons, and wrote the problem again: 25.0 grams of magnesium reacts with oxygen; how many moles of magnesium oxide form?

Her grandmother was at the counter slicing tomatoes for supper, reticent as always about Emma's schoolwork until it appeared on her table, at which point she tended to treat it like weather, something to be commented on and worked around. "You look like your father when he studied for his license," she said. "Same frown. He'd bite the pencil."

"I don't get where the grams go," Emma said. "Like, where do they go?"

"Grams of what?"

"Magnesium. It turns into magnesium oxide, and suddenly I'm supposed to count moles, and the numbers aren't even the same numbers."

Her grandmother set the knife down. She went to the pantry, that deep cool room that seemed to subsume half the house's history, jars of peaches and an old scale her grandfather had used for his honey, and came back with the scale and a ziplock bag from the box on top of the refrigerator. "Granddad's scale. Don't drop it."

"Grandma, I have to study."

"This is studying. Write your numbers down first, whatever they are."

Emma copied from her notes: Mg, 24.3 grams per mole. MgO, 40.3 grams per mole. Oxygen, 16.0. She said them aloud, and her grandmother put the empty bag on the scale and slid the little brass weights until the needle settled. "Twenty-six grams," her grandmother said, reading it, then watching Emma drop a coil of magnesium ribbon and a folded paper of some white powder from the chemistry kit into the bag and seal it. The needle didn't move. Twenty-six grams, sealed.

"So if it all reacted in there," Emma said slowly, "the bag would still weigh twenty-six grams. After."

"It better. Where would anything go? Bag's shut."

Emma stared at the needle. She had been imagining grams as disappearing into moles, some alchemy where the units were different currencies and mass got lost in the exchange like a fee. But if the reactants and the products weighed the same in a closed system, then nothing left, nothing vanished; the magnesium had to still be in the oxide, all of it, just married to oxygen it had pulled from the air in the bag. She did the arithmetic out loud. "25.0 grams of magnesium, and one mole of magnesium is 24.3 grams. So 25.0 divided by 24.3. That's 1.03 moles of magnesium."

"And one magnesium makes one magnesium oxide," her grandmother said, as if this were obvious, as if she were saying one cup of flour makes one loaf.

"One to one, they're both just Mg." Emma flipped to the back of her worksheet where the balanced equation waited, 2Mg + O2 goes to 2MgO, and yes, the ratio was one to one. So 1.03 moles of magnesium became 1.03 moles of magnesium oxide. She checked it against the mass the way you check a seam: 1.03 moles of MgO at 40.3 grams per mole was 41.5 grams of product, and the reactants were 25.0 grams of magnesium plus 16.5 grams of oxygen, which added to 41.5. The needle on the scale hadn't lied. The total mass of the products equaled the total mass of the reactants, exactly, because the bag was sealed and there was nowhere else for it to be.

"That's it?" she said. "That's the whole thing? You change grams to moles so you can count the particles, because particles are what react, and then you change back if you want grams?"

"I don't know about particles," her grandmother said, returning to her tomatoes. "But Granddad sold honey by the pound and made candles by the dozen, and he never confused the two, and he never lost a pound in the converting either."

Emma laughed, then wrote it out clean, the whole chain, so it would look like something she had always known. She underlined the answer, 1.03 moles, and felt the particular satisfaction of a method that closed on itself, though a small uncertainty stayed open in her like a door ajar: she could do the conversion now, but she couldn't quite see the particles themselves, couldn't picture the magnesium and the oxygen finding each other in the dark of the bag. She trusted the arithmetic more than the picture, and she wasn't sure yet whether that was a failure or just the beginning of how chemistry felt.

Her grandmother glanced at the notebook page. "That writing wants to be neater. Your teacher will mark you down."

"It's a quiz, not a calligraphy contest."

"Everything's a calligraphy contest in the end." She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at the sealed bag sitting on the counter, its coil of ribbon and its paper of powder waiting for some other lesson. Then she picked it up and set it on the scale again, the needle drifting, settling, holding steady at twenty-six.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
The community centre smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged into a rough horseshoe to stand in for a courtroom. Nicolas had signed up for the mock court program because the application for college debate had asked for extracurriculars, and this one met on Tuesdays, which were free. He had not read the assignment. Now it was Thursday, the exhibition was Saturday, and he sat at a table with Priya, who had already written fourteen pages.

"We're arguing Barnette," she said. "Both sides. Each of us argues for the school in round one and for the students in round two."

"That's insane."

"That's the point." She slid a photocopy across the table. "You can't just believe a thing. You have to be able to build the other side until it's strong enough to be worth beating."

Nicolas had assumed arguing was like fighting, and that the trouble with fighting was knowing which side you were on. He read the photocopy twice in the crepuscular light of the window, because half the overhead fluorescents were dead and nobody had reported it. In 1943, in West Virginia v. Barnette, the Supreme Court had ruled 6 to 3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Six justices against three, in the middle of a war, which Priya kept underlining as though the date itself were an argument.

A boy named Demarco, who was seventeen and had come only because his mother taught the pottery class down the hall, leaned over from the next table. "Wait, they can't make you stand for the pledge? Like actually can't?"

"That's the case," Priya said. "Six to three. Schools can't force it."

Demarco sat back. He had been made to stand, every morning, for three years, by a teacher who called it respect. He did not say this out loud, but he looked at the photocopy for a long time.

On Saturday the horseshoe filled with parents and a retired judge from the neighbourhood who agreed to sit in the middle chair. Nicolas argued for the school board first. He talked about unity, about children needing a common civic ritual, about a country at war asking for one small gesture. He built it carefully, the way Priya had shown him, until it sounded like something he might actually believe on a bad day. The judge nodded along. In the audience, Demarco watched him with an expression Nicolas could not read.

Then Priya stood for the students, and Nicolas had to cross-examine her. He asked whether a school could require anything at all, and she said the question was not whether schools could require things but whether they could require this. He pressed her on the idea that a salute was only symbolic, only words, and she quoted the line everyone quoted, about no official orthodoxy in matters of opinion, and for a moment the room went quiet in a way that felt physical, the parents transfixed by a sentence written before most of them were born.

In the second round the roles reversed, and Nicolas found himself arguing for the Barnette side, for the students who would not salute. He had expected it to feel like taking off a coat. Instead the school board's case kept rising in him, all the reasons he had built, and he had to set them down one at a time to make room. He lost his place once. He found it by looking at Demarco, who was now sitting forward with his arms on his knees.

Afterward the retired judge said both performances had merit and that Nicolas's second argument was the stronger one, though he had hesitated too long on the final question, and Nicolas could not tell whether the judge meant it or was being kind. The parents collected their coats. Priya began stacking chairs without being asked.

Demarco caught him at the door, by the water fountain that only produced a thin hot stream.

"So Monday," Demarco said, "when she tells me to stand."

Nicolas waited.

"Six to three," Demarco said. "That's real. That's actually the law."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of x to the power n is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1, for every n except negative 1.
story:
I have always understood things the first time. That is what I told my grandmother on the second morning, when she found me at her kitchen table with the calculus workbook she had bought in 1968 and never finished, and it was true, more or less, though the "less" had a habit of growing whenever I said it out loud.

The house sat at the end of a lane where a hedge circumscribed the entire garden, clipped so straight it looked ruled, and the only sounds were rooks and the occasional lorry on the far road, which made the teacups shiver in a small seismic way, as if the world were shrugging. My parents were forty miles away, unpacking boxes in the new house, and I had been parked here for the week like a piece of furniture too awkward to carry. I did not mind. Grandmother kept mints in a tin and asked no questions before noon.

The workbook was hers. She had left school at fifteen, and she had taught herself from this book, or started to; she was, she said, an autodidact of the interrupted kind. The pages were soft at the edges, and her handwriting ran in the margins, small and even, stopping abruptly at chapter six. I had chosen the book out of boredom and spite, because the fall term would put me in a class where the teacher had already decided I was average, and I wanted to walk in knowing things.

Integration was chapter six. The idea itself seemed almost friendly: you wanted the area under a curve, so you sliced it thin, and then you needed a way to add up infinitely many slices. The book gave a rule for it in a paragraph I can still recite. "The antiderivative of x to the power n," I read aloud, to the hedge and the rooks, "is x to the power n plus 1, divided by n plus 1." Then a small note, in parentheses, which I skipped, because I understood things the first time. I did forty minutes of exercises and filled three pages. The rule worked every time I used it. Powers folded themselves up neatly, like the laundry I refused to do.

Then I reached the curve y equals one over x. I knew enough to rewrite it as x to the power negative one, and I applied the rule the way you apply a rule, without looking at it. N plus one is zero. Zero in the denominator. The page stared back at me with a division by zero where an answer should have been, and I sat very still, because I had understood things the first time and this was not the first time, it was the forty-first, and it had waited until now to break.

In the afternoon my grandmother watched Victoria from the doorway for a while before she spoke. The girl had not moved from the table since breakfast except to fetch a second pencil, and the second pencil was now also worn to a stub. Grandmother knew that expression. Her late husband had worn it over the crossword, and she had worn it herself, in 1968, over this same chapter, which was why her handwriting stopped there. She brought the tea over and set it down without a saucer, which meant sit still and let me see.

"It doesn't work," Victoria said. "The rule. It works for everything and then it just doesn't."

"Read me the rule," Grandmother said. "Slowly. The way you read it this morning, with your eyes skipping."

Victoria read it again, and this time the parentheses caught her. "Every n except negative one," she said. "It says it right there. It was always saying it."

"So it was," said Grandmother, and she stole a mint from the tin and left the girl to it, because a person who finds the wall herself learns the shape of the room better than one who is carried around it.

Victoria stayed at the table until the light went long and orange across the ruled hedge. She could not explain why the exception existed, and the book did not either; it simply drew the boundary and moved on, the way a fence moves on past a tree it cannot pass through. She found she liked that. She liked the rule and she liked the hole in it, and she did not yet know how the two fit together, whether the hole was a failure of the rule or a door to something the rule could not reach. She copied the whole paragraph into her notebook, including the parentheses, and under the curve y equals one over x she wrote a question mark and boxed it twice.

That evening she told her mother on the phone that the week was going fine, that she had learned integration in an afternoon, first time, no trouble at all. Then she hung up, carried her tea to the window, and watched the rooks settle into the hedge while the box in her notebook waited on the table, small and dark, with its two careful lines drawn around it like a fence around a tree.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons, so averaging a full year of bills gives a truer monthly cost than a single month's bill.
story:
Wyatt sat on the bench at the corner of Fulton and Ninth with two printed leases folded in his back pocket, waiting for the 42 that would take him out to look at the second apartment before the landlord changed his mind about showing it at five o'clock. The first lease he had already read twice on his bed that morning: seven hundred a month, tenant pays all utilities. The second, the one in his pocket, was six-forty, and the listing said heat included, which sounded like the better deal until he tried to figure out how much better, and couldn't, and realized he didn't know what he was doing.

The bench had one other occupant, an old man with a folded newspaper and a thermos, who introduced himself as Gerald within the first minute and turned out to be a raconteur of the Fulton Street school, meaning that Wyatt now knew about the blizzard of '78, the fate of the hardware store that used to stand where the pharmacy is, and the precise way the 42 had been rerouted in 1994. Wyatt kept one ear on this and the other on his phone, where his grandfather was talking from his recliner in Phoenix, where he had gone to convalesce after the hip surgery and where, apparently, he had opinions about leases.

"You're looking at summer," his grandfather said. Wyatt had texted him a photo of the utility bills the first landlord had grudgingly provided, a stack of them, and his grandfather was scrolling through. "This one says forty-two dollars. You're thinking, forty-two dollars, that's nothing. That's July, Wyatt. Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons. A single month's bill will lie to you."

"So which month do I trust?"

"None of them. You add up the whole year, all twelve, and divide by twelve. That's the only number worth anything. A full year of bills, averaged, that's your truer monthly cost."

Gerald, who had been pretending to read his newspaper, lowered it. "Who's that telling you about bills?"

"My grandpa. I'm comparing two apartments."

"Compare away," Gerald said, with the ebullience of a man who had been starved for conversation since the newspaper ran out of surprises. "I paid rent on this street for forty years. Six-forty with heat included, that's the one you want, that's what I'd say, but I'd be guessing. I never once added up a year of anything."

Wyatt spread the bills on the bench between them, weighted the August one with his phone against the wind. The stack went back fourteen months. He added January, February, December, the numbers in the hundreds, then the shoulders of the seasons, then the summers, and the total came to something that divided out to just over ninety a month. Seven-ninety, effectively, for the first apartment. He wrote it on the back of the lease with a pen he had to shake.

"Still under eight hundred with utilities," his grandfather said. "Now the second one. What does heat included actually include?"

Wyatt read the clause out loud. Heat included meant the boiler, meant radiator steam; electricity was separate, and the listing estimated it at thirty-five. He did the arithmetic against the six-forty base rent and got six-seventy-five, and sat there looking at the two figures, one of which was built on twelve real bills and the other on a landlord's estimate of a single service in a single season, and understood that they were not the same kind of number at all. The first one had winter in it. The second one had an estimate.

"That electric estimate is probably summer too," his grandfather said. "You cool with electricity?"

"There's a window unit."

"Then your summer bills run high even with heat included, and there's no stack of bills to check it against. Ask him for the last tenant's electric bills. If he won't show you, that tells you something too."

The 42 came around the corner, brakes squealing, and Gerald stood and gathered his newspaper. "Tell me how it comes out," he said. "I'll be here tomorrow. I'm always here."

Wyatt boarded and took a window seat, the two leases in his lap, the one with twelve months of real history and the one with a promise and an estimate. He didn't know yet that the landlord would produce only three electric bills, all from spring, and would smile while doing it. He got off at the wrong stop on purpose and walked the last two blocks in the heat, doing the division again in his head, and when the landlord opened the door Wyatt said, "Before I look around, could I see the electric bills for the whole year?"
